texts.title: Miss Brill (opening)
texts.author: Katherine Mansfield
texts.source: From “Miss Brill” in The Garden Party, and Other Stories by Katherine Mansfield (20th-century short story). Project Gutenberg #1429. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Although it was so brilliantly fine—the blue sky powdered with gold and
great spots of light like white wine splashed over the Jardins
Publiques—Miss Brill was glad that she had decided on her fur. The air
was motionless, but when you opened your mouth there was just a faint
chill, like a chill from a glass of iced water before you sip, and now
and again a leaf came drifting—from nowhere, from the sky. Miss Brill
put up her hand and touched her fur. Dear little thing! It was nice to
feel it again. She had taken it out of its box that afternoon, shaken
out the moth-powder, given it a good brush, and rubbed the life back
into the dim little eyes. “What has been happening to me?” said the sad
little eyes. Oh, how sweet it was to see them snap at her again from the
red eiderdown!... But the nose, which was of some black composition,
wasn’t at all firm. It must have had a knock, somehow. Never mind—a
little dab of black sealing-wax when the time came—when it was
absolutely necessary.... Little rogue! Yes, she really felt like that
about it. Little rogue biting its tail just by her left ear. She could
have taken it off and laid it on her lap and stroked it. She felt a
tingling in her hands and arms, but that came from walking, she
supposed. And when she breathed, something light and sad—no, not sad,
exactly—something gentle seemed to move in her bosom.
glossary: wax once used to seal letters

texts.title: The Garden-Party (opening)
texts.author: Katherine Mansfield
texts.source: From “The Garden-Party” in The Garden Party, and Other Stories by Katherine Mansfield (20th-century short story). Project Gutenberg #1429. Public domain in the UK.
lines: And after all the weather was ideal. They could not have had a more
perfect day for a garden-party if they had ordered it. Windless, warm,
the sky without a cloud. Only the blue was veiled with a haze of light
gold, as it is sometimes in early summer. The gardener had been up since
dawn, mowing the lawns and sweeping them, until the grass and the dark
flat rosettes where the daisy plants had been seemed to shine. As for
the roses, you could not help feeling they understood that roses are the
only flowers that impress people at garden-parties; the only flowers
that everybody is certain of knowing. Hundreds, yes, literally hundreds,
had come out in a single night; the green bushes bowed down as though
they had been visited by archangels.
Breakfast was not yet over before the men came to put up the marquee.
“Where do you want the marquee put, mother?”
“My dear child, it’s no use asking me. I’m determined to leave
everything to you children this year. Forget I am your mother. Treat me
as an honoured guest.”
But Meg could not possibly go and supervise the men. She had washed her
hair before breakfast, and she sat drinking her coffee in a green
turban, with a dark wet curl stamped on each cheek.
glossary: a large tent put up for a party
a cloth wrapped round the head

texts.title: Her First Ball (opening)
texts.author: Katherine Mansfield
texts.source: From “Her First Ball” in The Garden Party, and Other Stories by Katherine Mansfield (20th-century short story). Project Gutenberg #1429. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Exactly when the ball began Leila would have found it hard to say.
Perhaps her first real partner was the cab. It did not matter that she
shared the cab with the Sheridan girls and their brother. She sat back
in her own little corner of it, and the bolster on which her hand rested
felt like the sleeve of an unknown young man’s dress suit; and away they
bowled, past waltzing lamp-posts and houses and fences and trees.
“Have you really never been to a ball before, Leila? But, my child, how
too weird—” cried the Sheridan girls.
“Our nearest neighbour was fifteen miles,” said Leila softly, gently
opening and shutting her fan.
Oh dear, how hard it was to be indifferent like the others! She tried
not to smile too much; she tried not to care. But every single thing was
so new and exciting... Meg’s tuberoses, Jose’s long loop of amber,
Laura’s little dark head, pushing above her white fur like a flower
through snow. She would remember for ever. It even gave her a pang to
see her cousin Laurie throw away the wisps of tissue paper he pulled
from the fastenings of his new gloves. She would like to have kept those
wisps as a keepsake, as a remembrance.
glossary: a golden stone used for beads

texts.title: The Voyage (opening)
texts.author: Katherine Mansfield
texts.source: From “The Voyage” in The Garden Party, and Other Stories by Katherine Mansfield (20th-century short story). Project Gutenberg #1429. Public domain in the UK.
lines: The Picton boat was due to leave at half-past eleven. It was a beautiful
night, mild, starry, only when they got out of the cab and started to
walk down the Old Wharf that jutted out into the harbour, a faint wind
blowing off the water ruffled under Fenella’s hat, and she put up her
hand to keep it on. It was dark on the Old Wharf, very dark; the wool
sheds, the cattle trucks, the cranes standing up so high, the little
squat railway engine, all seemed carved out of solid darkness. Here and
there on a rounded wood-pile, that was like the stalk of a huge black
mushroom, there hung a lantern, but it seemed afraid to unfurl its
timid, quivering light in all that blackness; it burned softly, as if
for itself.
Fenella’s father pushed on with quick, nervous strides. Beside him her
grandma bustled along in her crackling black ulster; they went so fast
that she had now and again to give an undignified little skip to keep up
with them. As well as her luggage strapped into a neat sausage, Fenella
carried clasped to her her grandma’s umbrella, and the handle, which was
a swan’s head, kept giving her shoulder a sharp little peck as if it too
wanted her to hurry.... Men, their caps pulled down, their collars
turned up, swung by; a few women all muffled scurried along; and one
tiny boy, only his little black arms and legs showing out of a white
woolly shawl, was jerked along angrily between his father and mother; he
looked like a baby fly that had fallen into the cream.
glossary: a platform where boats tie up

texts.title: Jacob’s Room (opening)
texts.author: Virginia Woolf
texts.source: From Jacob’s Room by Virginia Woolf (20th-century novel). Project Gutenberg #5670. Public domain in the UK.
lines: "So of course," wrote Betty Flanders, pressing her heels rather deeper
in the sand, "there was nothing for it but to leave."
Slowly welling from the point of her gold nib, pale blue ink dissolved
the full stop; for there her pen stuck; her eyes fixed, and tears slowly
filled them. The entire bay quivered; the lighthouse wobbled; and she
had the illusion that the mast of Mr. Connor's little yacht was bending
like a wax candle in the sun. She winked quickly. Accidents were awful
things. She winked again. The mast was straight; the waves were regular;
the lighthouse was upright; but the blot had spread.
"... nothing for it but to leave," she read.
"Well, if Jacob doesn't want to play" (the shadow of Archer, her eldest
son, fell across the notepaper and looked blue on the sand, and she felt
chilly--it was the third of September already), "if Jacob doesn't want
to play"--what a horrid blot! It must be getting late.
"Where IS that tiresome little boy?" she said. "I don't see him. Run and
find him. Tell him to come at once." "... but mercifully," she
scribbled, ignoring the full stop, "everything seems satisfactorily
arranged, packed though we are like herrings in a barrel, and forced to
stand the perambulator which the landlady quite naturally won't
allow...."
Such were Betty Flanders's letters to Captain Barfoot--many-paged,
tear-stained. Scarborough is seven hundred miles from Cornwall: Captain
Barfoot is in Scarborough: Seabrook is dead. Tears made all the dahlias
in her garden undulate in red waves and flashed the glass house in her
eyes, and spangled the kitchen with bright knives, and made Mrs. Jarvis,
the rector's wife, think at church, while the hymn-tune played and Mrs.
Flanders bent low over her little boys' heads, that marriage is a
fortress and widows stray solitary in the open fields, picking up
stones, gleaning a few golden straws, lonely, unprotected, poor
creatures. Mrs. Flanders had been a widow for these two years.
glossary: the metal point of a pen

texts.title: Mrs Dalloway (opening)
texts.author: Virginia Woolf
texts.source: From Mrs. Dalloway by Virginia Woolf (20th-century novel, 1925). Project Gutenberg #71865. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.
For Lucy had her work cut out for her. The doors would be taken off
their hinges; Rumpelmayer’s men were coming. And then, thought Clarissa
Dalloway, what a morning--fresh as if issued to children on a beach.
What a lark! What a plunge! For so it had always seemed to her, when,
with a little squeak of the hinges, which she could hear now, she had
burst open the French windows and plunged at Bourton into the open air.
How fresh, how calm, stiller than this of course, the air was in the
early morning; like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and
sharp and yet (for a girl of eighteen as she then was) solemn, feeling
as she did, standing there at the open window, that something awful was
about to happen; looking at the flowers, at the trees with the smoke
winding off them and the rooks rising, falling; standing and looking
until Peter Walsh said, “Musing among the vegetables?”--was that it?--“I
prefer men to cauliflowers”--was that it? He must have said it at
breakfast one morning when she had gone out on to the terrace--Peter
Walsh. He would be back from India one of these days, June or July, she
forgot which, for his letters were awfully dull; it was his sayings one
remembered; his eyes, his pocket-knife, his smile, his grumpiness and,
when millions of things had utterly vanished--how strange it was!--a few
sayings like this about cabbages.
She stiffened a little on the kerb, waiting for Durtnall’s van to pass.
A charming woman, Scrope Purvis thought her (knowing her as one does
know people who live next door to one in Westminster); a touch of the
bird about her, of the jay, blue-green, light, vivacious, though she was
over fifty, and grown very white since her illness. There she perched,
never seeing him, waiting to cross, very upright.
glossary: the country house where Clarissa grew up

texts.title: The Streets: Morning
texts.author: Charles Dickens
texts.source: From “The Streets—Morning” in Sketches by Boz by Charles Dickens (19th-century sketch of London life). Project Gutenberg #882. Public domain in the UK.
lines: The last drunken man, who shall find his way home before sunlight, has
just staggered heavily along, roaring out the burden of the drinking
song of the previous night: the last houseless vagrant whom penury and
police have left in the streets, has coiled up his chilly limbs in some
paved comer, to dream of food and warmth. The drunken, the dissipated,
and the wretched have disappeared; the more sober and orderly part of
the population have not yet awakened to the labours of the day, and the
stillness of death is over the streets; its very hue seems to be
imparted to them, cold and lifeless as they look in the grey, sombre
light of daybreak. The coach-stands in the larger thoroughfares are
deserted: the night-houses are closed; and the chosen promenades of
profligate misery are empty.
An occasional policeman may alone be seen at the street corners,
listlessly gazing on the deserted prospect before him; and now and then
a rakish-looking cat runs stealthily across the road and descends his
own area with as much caution and slyness—bounding first on the
water-butt, then on the dust-hole, and then alighting on the
flag-stones—as if he were conscious that his character depended on his
gallantry of the preceding night escaping public observation. A
partially opened bedroom-window here and there, bespeaks the heat of the
weather, and the uneasy slumbers of its occupant; and the dim scanty
flicker of the rushlight, through the window-blind, denotes the chamber
of watching or sickness. With these few exceptions, the streets present
no signs of life, nor the houses of habitation.
glossary: the sunken yard in front of a basement

texts.title: Watercress Girl
texts.author: Henry Mayhew
texts.source: From London Labour and the London Poor, Vol. 1 by Henry Mayhew (19th-century journalism, first published 1851). Project Gutenberg #55998. Public domain in the UK.
lines: The little watercress girl who gave me the following statement, although
only eight years of age, had entirely lost all childish ways, and was,
indeed, in thoughts and manner, a woman. There was something cruelly
pathetic in hearing this infant, so young that her features had scarcely
formed themselves, talking of the bitterest struggles of life, with the
calm earnestness of one who had endured them all. I did not know how to
talk with her. At first I treated her as a child, speaking on childish
subjects; so that I might, by being familiar with her, remove all
shyness, and get her to narrate her life freely. I asked her about her
toys and her games with her companions; but the look of amazement that
answered me soon put an end to any attempt at fun on my part. I then
talked to her about the parks, and whether she ever went to them. “The
parks!” she replied in wonder, “where are they?” I explained to her,
telling her that they were large open places with green grass and tall
trees, where beautiful carriages drove about, and people walked for
pleasure, and children played. Her eyes brightened up a little as I
spoke; and she asked, half doubtingly, “Would they let such as me go
there--just to look?” All her knowledge seemed to begin and end with
water-cresses, and what they fetched. She knew no more of London than
that part she had seen on her rounds, and believed that no quarter of
the town was handsomer or pleasanter than it was at Farringdon-market or
at Clerkenwell, where she lived. Her little face, pale and thin with
privation, was wrinkled where the dimples ought to have been, and she
would sigh frequently. When some hot dinner was offered to her, she
would not touch it, because, if she eat too much, “it made her sick,”
she said; “and she wasn’t used to meat, only on a Sunday.”
glossary: a London market where watercress was sold

texts.title: The Voyage Out (opening)
texts.author: Virginia Woolf
texts.source: From The Voyage Out by Virginia Woolf (20th-century novel). Project Gutenberg #144. Public domain in the UK.
lines: As the streets that lead from the Strand to the Embankment are very
narrow, it is better not to walk down them arm-in-arm. If you persist,
lawyers’ clerks will have to make flying leaps into the mud; young lady
typists will have to fidget behind you. In the streets of London where
beauty goes unregarded, eccentricity must pay the penalty, and it is
better not to be very tall, to wear a long blue cloak, or to beat the
air with your left hand.
One afternoon in the beginning of October when the traffic was becoming
brisk a tall man strode along the edge of the pavement with a lady on
his arm. Angry glances struck upon their backs. The small, agitated
figures—for in comparison with this couple most people looked
small—decorated with fountain pens, and burdened with despatch-boxes,
had appointments to keep, and drew a weekly salary, so that there was
some reason for the unfriendly stare which was bestowed upon Mr.
Ambrose’s height and upon Mrs. Ambrose’s cloak. But some enchantment had
put both man and woman beyond the reach of malice and unpopularity. In
his case one might guess from the moving lips that it was thought; and
in hers from the eyes fixed stonily straight in front of her at a level
above the eyes of most that it was sorrow. It was only by scorning all
she met that she kept herself from tears, and the friction of people
brushing past her was evidently painful. After watching the traffic on
the Embankment for a minute or two with a stoical gaze she twitched her
husband’s sleeve, and they crossed between the swift discharge of motor
cars. When they were safe on the further side, she gently withdrew her
arm from his, allowing her mouth at the same time to relax, to tremble;
then tears rolled down, and leaning her elbows on the balustrade, she
shielded her face from the curious. Mr. Ambrose attempted consolation;
he patted her shoulder; but she showed no signs of admitting him, and
feeling it awkward to stand beside a grief that was greater than his, he
crossed his arms behind him, and took a turn along the pavement.
glossary: places in central London near the River Thames

texts.title: The Prussian Officer (opening)
texts.author: D. H. Lawrence
texts.source: From “The Prussian Officer” in The Prussian Officer and Other Stories by D. H. Lawrence (20th-century short story, published 1914). Project Gutenberg #22480. Public domain in the UK.
lines: They had marched more than thirty kilometres since dawn, along the
white, hot road where occasional thickets of trees threw a moment of
shade, then out into the glare again. On either hand, the valley, wide
and shallow, glittered with heat; dark green patches of rye, pale young
corn, fallow and meadow and black pine woods spread in a dull, hot
diagram under a glistening sky. But right in front the mountains ranged
across, pale blue and very still, snow gleaming gently out of the deep
atmosphere. And towards the mountains, on and on, the regiment marched
between the rye fields and the meadows, between the scraggy fruit trees
set regularly on either side the high road. The burnished, dark green
rye threw on a suffocating heat, the mountains drew gradually nearer and
more distinct. While the feet of the soldiers grew hotter, sweat ran
through their hair under their helmets, and their knapsacks could burn
no more in contact with their shoulders, but seemed instead to give off
a cold, prickly sensation.
He walked on and on in silence, staring at the mountains ahead, that
rose sheer out of the land, and stood fold behind fold, half earth, half
heaven, the heaven, the banner with slits of soft snow, in the pale,
bluish peaks.
He could now walk almost without pain. At the start, he had determined
not to limp. It had made him sick to take the first steps, and during
the first mile or so, he had compressed his breath, and the cold drops
of sweat had stood on his forehead. But he had walked it off. What were
they after all but bruises! He had looked at them, as he was getting up:
deep bruises on the backs of his thighs. And since he had made his first
step in the morning, he had been conscious of them, till now he had a
tight, hot place in his chest, with suppressing the pain, and holding
himself in. There seemed no air when he breathed. But he walked almost
lightly.

texts.title: To Build a Fire (the fire)
texts.author: Jack London
texts.source: From “To Build a Fire” in Lost Face by Jack London (20th-century short story; UK edition first published 1916). Project Gutenberg #2429. Public domain in the UK.
lines: But he was safe. Toes and nose and cheeks would be only touched by the
frost, for the fire was beginning to burn with strength. He was feeding
it with twigs the size of his finger. In another minute he would be able
to feed it with branches the size of his wrist, and then he could remove
his wet foot-gear, and, while it dried, he could keep his naked feet
warm by the fire, rubbing them at first, of course, with snow. The fire
was a success. He was safe. He remembered the advice of the old-timer on
Sulphur Creek, and smiled. The old-timer had been very serious in laying
down the law that no man must travel alone in the Klondike after fifty
below. Well, here he was; he had had the accident; he was alone; and he
had saved himself. Those old-timers were rather womanish, some of them,
he thought. All a man had to do was to keep his head, and he was all
right. Any man who was a man could travel alone. But it was surprising,
the rapidity with which his cheeks and nose were freezing. And he had
not thought his fingers could go lifeless in so short a time. Lifeless
they were, for he could scarcely make them move together to grip a twig,
and they seemed remote from his body and from him. When he touched a
twig, he had to look and see whether or not he had hold of it. The wires
were pretty well down between him and his finger-ends.
All of which counted for little. There was the fire, snapping and
crackling and promising life with every dancing flame. He started to
untie his moccasins. They were coated with ice; the thick German socks
were like sheaths of iron half-way to the knees; and the mocassin
strings were like rods of steel all twisted and knotted as by some
conflagration. For a moment he tugged with his numbed fingers, then,
realizing the folly of it, he drew his sheath-knife.
But before he could cut the strings, it happened. It was his own fault
or, rather, his mistake. He should not have built the fire under the
spruce tree. He should have built it in the open. But it had been easier
to pull the twigs from the brush and drop them directly on the fire. Now
the tree under which he had done this carried a weight of snow on its
boughs. No wind had blown for weeks, and each bough was fully freighted.
Each time he had pulled a twig he had communicated a slight agitation to
the tree—an imperceptible agitation, so far as he was concerned, but an
agitation sufficient to bring about the disaster. High up in the tree
one bough capsized its load of snow. This fell on the boughs beneath,
capsizing them. This process continued, spreading out and involving the
whole tree. It grew like an avalanche, and it descended without warning
upon the man and the fire, and the fire was blotted out! Where it had
burned was a mantle of fresh and disordered snow.
glossary: a freezing region of north-west Canada

texts.title: Bliss (opening)
texts.author: Katherine Mansfield
texts.source: From “Bliss” in Bliss, and Other Stories by Katherine Mansfield (20th-century short story, published 1920). Project Gutenberg #44385. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Although Bertha Young was thirty she still had moments like this when
she wanted to run instead of walk, to take dancing steps on and off the
pavement, to bowl a hoop, to throw something up in the air and catch it
again, or to stand still and laugh at—nothing—at nothing, simply.
What can you do if you are thirty and, turning the corner of your own
street, you are overcome, suddenly, by a feeling of bliss—absolute
bliss!—as though you’d suddenly swallowed a bright piece of that late
afternoon sun and it burned in your bosom, sending out a little shower
of sparks into every particle, into every finger and toe? . . .
Oh, is there no way you can express it without being “drunk and
disorderly”? How idiotic civilization is! Why be given a body if you
have to keep it shut up in a case like a rare, rare fiddle?
“No, that about the fiddle is not quite what I mean,” she thought,
running up the steps and feeling in her bag for the key—she’d forgotten
it, as usual—and rattling the letter-box. “It’s not what I mean,
because—— Thank you, Mary”—she went into the hall. “Is nurse back?”
“Yes, M’m.”
“And has the fruit come?”
“Yes, M’m. Everything’s come.”
“Bring the fruit up to the dining-room, will you? I’ll arrange it before
I go upstairs.”
It was dusky in the dining-room and quite chilly. But all the same
Bertha threw off her coat; she could not bear the tight clasp of it
another moment, and the cold air fell on her arms.
glossary: a children’s game: rolling a hoop along with a stick
a legal charge for bad behaviour in public

texts.title: Travels with a Donkey: the sleeping-sack
texts.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
texts.source: From Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes by Robert Louis Stevenson (19th-century travel writing). Project Gutenberg #535. Public domain in the UK.
lines: It was already hard upon October before I was ready to set forth, and at
the high altitudes over which my road lay there was no Indian summer to
be looked for. I was determined, if not to camp out, at least to have
the means of camping out in my possession; for there is nothing more
harassing to an easy mind than the necessity of reaching shelter by
dusk, and the hospitality of a village inn is not always to be reckoned
sure by those who trudge on foot. A tent, above all for a solitary
traveller, is troublesome to pitch, and troublesome to strike again; and
even on the march it forms a conspicuous feature in your baggage. A
sleeping-sack, on the other hand, is always ready--you have only to get
into it; it serves a double purpose--a bed by night, a portmanteau by
day; and it does not advertise your intention of camping out to every
curious passer-by. This is a huge point. If a camp is not secret, it is
but a troubled resting-place; you become a public character; the
convivial rustic visits your bedside after an early supper; and you must
sleep with one eye open, and be up before the day. I decided on a
sleeping-sack; and after repeated visits to Le Puy, and a deal of high
living for myself and my advisers, a sleeping-sack was designed,
constructed, and triumphantly brought home.
This child of my invention was nearly six feet square, exclusive of two
triangular flaps to serve as a pillow by night and as the top and bottom
of the sack by day. I call it 'the sack,' but it was never a sack by
more than courtesy: only a sort of long roll or sausage, green
waterproof cart-cloth without and blue sheep's fur within. It was
commodious as a valise, warm and dry for a bed.
glossary: a spell of warm weather in autumn

texts.title: Cabins at sea
texts.author: Source A: Inkworks Press; Source B: Charles Dickens
texts.source: Source A: “Deck 8”, a 21st-century travel article. Written for Inkworks Press. Source B: from American Notes by Charles Dickens (19th-century travel writing about a voyage made in January 1842). Project Gutenberg #675. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Source A: “Deck 8”, a travel article about an overnight ferry (21st century)
Cabin 8127 is on deck 8, halfway along a corridor so long that it seems
to bend. The card key works first time, and a strip light flickers on
before I have found the switch. A pair of narrow bunks fold down from
the walls, already made up with white sheets tucked as tight as
envelopes.
There is no porthole. Instead, a small screen above the desk shows a
live picture from a camera on the bow: black water and a smear of
harbour lights. The shower room is a moulded plastic pod the size of a
phone box, where everything is bolted down or clipped in place.
Somewhere beneath the carpet the engines hum, steady and faint, like a
fridge in another room.
I have paid £89 for 11 hours in here, and by midnight I am grateful for
every square metre. It is not beautiful. It is clean and warm, and after
a day of queues that feels close to luxury.
Source B: Charles Dickens boards a steamship to America (19th century)
I SHALL never forget the one-fourth serious and three-fourths comical
astonishment, with which, on the morning of the third of January
eighteen-hundred-and-forty-two, I opened the door of, and put my head
into, a ‘state-room’ on board the Britannia steam-packet, twelve hundred
tons burthen per register, bound for Halifax and Boston, and carrying
Her Majesty’s mails.
That this state-room had been specially engaged for ‘Charles Dickens,
Esquire, and Lady,’ was rendered sufficiently clear even to my scared
intellect by a very small manuscript, announcing the fact, which was
pinned on a very flat quilt, covering a very thin mattress, spread like
a surgical plaster on a most inaccessible shelf.
glossary: a steamship carrying mail and passengers
an old word for a ship’s carrying capacity

texts.title: The Voyage of the Beagle: a Brazilian forest
texts.author: Charles Darwin
texts.source: From The Voyage of the Beagle by Charles Darwin (19th-century travel journal). Project Gutenberg #944. Public domain in the UK.
lines: BAHIA, OR SAN SALVADOR. BRAZIL, Feb. 29th.--The day has passed
delightfully. Delight itself, however, is a weak term to express the
feelings of a naturalist who, for the first time, has wandered by
himself in a Brazilian forest. The elegance of the grasses, the novelty
of the parasitical plants, the beauty of the flowers, the glossy green
of the foliage, but above all the general luxuriance of the vegetation,
filled me with admiration. A most paradoxical mixture of sound and
silence pervades the shady parts of the wood. The noise from the insects
is so loud, that it may be heard even in a vessel anchored several
hundred yards from the shore; yet within the recesses of the forest a
universal silence appears to reign. To a person fond of natural history,
such a day as this brings with it a deeper pleasure than he can ever
hope to experience again. After wandering about for some hours, I
returned to the landing-place; but, before reaching it, I was overtaken
by a tropical storm. I tried to find shelter under a tree, which was so
thick that it would never have been penetrated by common English rain;
but here, in a couple of minutes, a little torrent flowed down the
trunk. It is to this violence of the rain that we must attribute the
verdure at the bottom of the thickest woods: if the showers were like
those of a colder climate, the greater part would be absorbed or
evaporated before it reached the ground.
glossary: a scientist who studies plants and animals
plants that grow on other plants

texts.title: Help and self-help
texts.author: Source A: Inkworks Press; Source B: Samuel Smiles
texts.source: Source A: “Who held the rope?”, a 21st-century opinion column. Written for Inkworks Press. Source B: from Self-Help by Samuel Smiles (19th-century book, first published 1859). Project Gutenberg #935. Public domain in the UK.
lines: Source A: “Who held the rope?”, an opinion column (21st century)
When people ask how I became the first person in my family to go to
university, they seem to want a story about grit. I understand why. It
is a tidy story, and it flatters everybody who tells it. But it is not
quite true.
I did work hard. I also had a maths teacher, Mrs Okafor, who stayed
behind on Thursdays for anyone who turned up. There was a library 10
minutes from my flat that stayed warm and quiet until 8pm. When my mum
lost her job in Year 11, a bursary paid for my bus pass, and an older
cousin read my university application 5 times. Take away any one of
those and I am not sure the effort would have been enough.
We like to believe that effort is the whole answer because it puts
success within everyone’s reach. Yet effort needs somewhere to happen. A
teenager revising at a kitchen table while 3 younger siblings watch
cartoons is working just as hard as one with a desk and a door that
shuts. The difference is not character.
So by all means praise the climber. Just remember who held the rope.
Source B: from Self-Help by Samuel Smiles (19th century)
“HEAVEN helps those who help themselves” is a well-tried maxim,
embodying in a small compass the results of vast human experience. The
spirit of self-help is the root of all genuine growth in the individual;
and, exhibited in the lives of many, it constitutes the true source of
national vigour and strength. Help from without is often enfeebling in
its effects, but help from within invariably invigorates. Whatever is
done for men or classes, to a certain extent takes away the stimulus and
necessity of doing for themselves; and where men are subjected to
over-guidance and over-government, the inevitable tendency is to render
them comparatively helpless.
Even the best institutions can give a man no active help. Perhaps the
most they can do is, to leave him free to develop himself and improve
his individual condition. But in all times men have been prone to
believe that their happiness and well-being were to be secured by means
of institutions rather than by their own conduct.
glossary: a short saying that gives advice
organisations such as governments, charities and schools

texts.title: A student’s description: the bus station
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A student-style description containing 1 deliberate punctuation error.
lines: The bus station was empty. Well, nearly empty. A cleaner pushed a wide
broom along the far platform, and the bristles made a dry, scratching
whisper that followed her like a shadow.
Above the ticket office a clock had stopped at 4.17, its hands folded
together as if it had given up waiting, the departures board flickered,
orange letters appearing and disappearing, promising buses to places
nobody was going.
I could smell diesel and cold coffee. A pigeon walked in a slow circle
round a dropped crust, too proud to hurry. Somewhere a radio was playing
very quietly, a song I almost knew.
Outside, the sky over the multi-storey car park was turning the colour
of weak tea. A taxi waited by the kerb with its engine running, the
driver asleep with his cap pulled down.
Then the first bus arrived. Its headlights swept across the concrete and
for a moment every puddle was full of light. The doors sighed open.
Nobody got off.

texts.title: A 5-minute plan for Paper 2 Question 5
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press.
lines: Task: ‘Teenagers should be paid for good exam results.’ Write an article
for a news website in which you argue for or against this statement.
Viewpoint: against. The reward should be the learning, not a payment.
Audience: adults and teenagers reading a news website, so formal but
lively.
Opening: a scene. A Year 11 student works out how much cash she could
earn for a grade 7.
Paragraph 2: money changes why people learn. Once the payments stop, the
effort stops.
Paragraph 3: it rewards students who already have advantages, such as a
quiet room and a tutor.
Paragraph 4: the other side. Some parents say it motivates. Reply: the
effect is short-term, and it turns school into a job.
Paragraph 5: what would help instead, such as free revision sessions and
useful feedback.
Ending: return to the student from the opening, now choosing a subject
because she enjoys it.
Check: leave 5 minutes to proofread for full stops and spelling.

texts.title: Fix it, don’t bin it
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A 21st-century opinion article.
lines: On the first Saturday of every month, the church hall on Mill Lane fills
with broken things. There are toasters that no longer toast and lamps
that flicker. Their owners queue with a mixture of hope and
embarrassment, because most of them have already been told the item is
not worth fixing.
That advice is often wrong. At our town’s repair café, volunteers mend
most of what comes through the door. Many faults are small, such as a
loose wire or a worn belt. The skill involved is real, but it can be
learned in an afternoon.
However, the café is about more than saving money. Every repaired kettle
is one less thing in landfill. As a result, the volunteers keep a
running tally on a whiteboard by the door, and they cheer when it goes
up.
Meanwhile, something harder to count happens at the tables. Strangers
sit side by side, watching a retired engineer coax a radio back to life,
and they start talking. A teenager shows a pensioner how to update a
phone. The pensioner shows the teenager how to sew on a button.
This is why every town should have a repair café. It costs very little
to run, and it turns a pile of broken things into a room full of people
who are glad they came.
So next time the toaster stops toasting, do not throw it away. Bring it
to Mill Lane.

texts.title: Kew Gardens (opening)
texts.author: Virginia Woolf
texts.source: From “Kew Gardens” in Monday or Tuesday by Virginia Woolf (20th-century short story; collection published 1921). Project Gutenberg #29220. Public domain in the UK.
lines: From the oval-shaped flower-bed there rose perhaps a hundred stalks
spreading into heart-shaped or tongue-shaped leaves half way up and
unfurling at the tip red or blue or yellow petals marked with spots of
colour raised upon the surface; and from the red, blue or yellow gloom
of the throat emerged a straight bar, rough with gold dust and slightly
clubbed at the end. The petals were voluminous enough to be stirred by
the summer breeze, and when they moved, the red, blue and yellow lights
passed one over the other, staining an inch of the brown earth beneath
with a spot of the most intricate colour. The light fell either upon the
smooth, grey back of a pebble, or, the shell of a snail with its brown,
circular veins, or falling into a raindrop, it expanded with such
intensity of red, blue and yellow the thin walls of water that one
expected them to burst and disappear. Instead, the drop was left in a
second silver grey once more, and the light now settled upon the flesh
of a leaf, revealing the branching thread of fibre beneath the surface,
and again it moved on and spread its illumination in the vast green
spaces beneath the dome of the heart-shaped and tongue-shaped leaves.
Then the breeze stirred rather more briskly overhead and the colour was
flashed into the air above, into the eyes of the men and women who walk
in Kew Gardens in July.
The figures of these men and women straggled past the flower-bed with a
curiously irregular movement not unlike that of the white and blue
butterflies who crossed the turf in zig-zag flights from bed to bed. The
man was about six inches in front of the woman, strolling carelessly,
while she bore on with greater purpose, only turning her head now and
then to see that the children were not too far behind. The man kept this
distance in front of the woman purposely, though perhaps unconsciously,
for he wished to go on with his thoughts.

texts.title: The Thirty-Nine Steps (opening)
texts.author: John Buchan
texts.source: From The Thirty-Nine Steps by John Buchan (20th-century novel, published 1915). Project Gutenberg #558. Public domain in the UK.
lines: I returned from the City about three o’clock on that May afternoon
pretty well disgusted with life. I had been three months in the Old
Country, and was fed up with it. If anyone had told me a year ago that I
would have been feeling like that I should have laughed at him; but
there was the fact. The weather made me liverish, the talk of the
ordinary Englishman made me sick. I couldn’t get enough exercise, and
the amusements of London seemed as flat as soda-water that has been
standing in the sun. “Richard Hannay,” I kept telling myself, “you have
got into the wrong ditch, my friend, and you had better climb out.”
It made me bite my lips to think of the plans I had been building up
those last years in Buluwayo. I had got my pile—not one of the big ones,
but good enough for me; and I had figured out all kinds of ways of
enjoying myself. My father had brought me out from Scotland at the age
of six, and I had never been home since; so England was a sort of
Arabian Nights to me, and I counted on stopping there for the rest of my
days.
But from the first I was disappointed with it. In about a week I was
tired of seeing sights, and in less than a month I had had enough of
restaurants and theatres and race-meetings. I had no real pal to go
about with, which probably explains things. Plenty of people invited me
to their houses, but they didn’t seem much interested in me. They would
fling me a question or two about South Africa, and then get on to their
own affairs. A lot of Imperialist ladies asked me to tea to meet
schoolmasters from New Zealand and editors from Vancouver, and that was
the dismalest business of all. Here was I, thirty-seven years old, sound
in wind and limb, with enough money to have a good time, yawning my head
off all day. I had just about settled to clear out and get back to the
veld, for I was the best bored man in the United Kingdom.
glossary: a city in southern Africa (now spelt Bulawayo)

texts.title: Give us back our lunch hour
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A 21st-century opinion article for a school website.
lines: At 12.40 the bell goes. By 12.45 the queue for the canteen stretches
past the library. By the time most of us sit down, we have 15 minutes to
eat and get to the other side of the site. Nobody calls that a break. It
is a pit stop.
Our school cut lunch to 35 minutes last year so that the day could
finish earlier. I understand the thinking. Buses are easier to arrange,
and some students have jobs or younger siblings to collect. But the
change has cost us something that does not show up on a timetable.
Lunch used to be when things happened. The chess club met. The football
pitch was full. The Year 7s learned where the music rooms were by
following older students there. Teachers ran catch-up sessions for
anyone who was stuck. Now the clubs have shrunk and the corridors are a
scramble.
Some will say a longer lunch simply means more time for trouble. Ask any
teacher on duty, though, and they will tell you that the worst behaviour
comes from students who are hungry and rushed. Give people time and most
of them use it well.
So here is my proposal: return lunch to 1 hour, and finish the day 25
minutes later. It is a small price for a school that feels like a
community again. We are not asking for a longer holiday. We are asking
for time to eat.

texts.title: A letter to the editor
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A 21st-century letter to a local newspaper.
lines: Dear Editor,
I am writing about last week’s report that the number 42 bus will stop
running after 7pm from September.
The council describes the evening service as ‘underused’. I would invite
any councillor to ride it on a Thursday. They would meet nurses
finishing a shift at the hospital and students coming home from college.
They would meet my grandmother, who has not driven for 10 years and
relies on it to get back from her choir.
For many of us, the 42 is not a convenience. It is the only way home.
Without it, some people will pay for taxis they cannot afford. Others
will simply stop going out after dark.
I accept that the council has hard choices to make. However, cutting a
service used by people with no other option is a false saving. It moves
the cost from the council’s budget to the pockets of those least able to
pay.
I urge readers to respond to the consultation before it closes at the
end of the month, and I urge the council to think again.
Yours faithfully,
Priya Chauhan (Year 11 student)

texts.title: A speech to the council
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A 21st-century speech to a town council meeting.
lines: Good evening, councillors. My name is Daniel Evans, and I am 16. I have
lived in this town all my life.
Tonight you will decide what happens to the empty land behind the
leisure centre. I am here to ask you to build a skate park on it.
Look around this town after school. Where are young people supposed to
go? The benches outside the shops, or the car park by the station? We
get moved on from both, and I understand why. But moving us on does not
give us anywhere to go.
A skate park would. It would be somewhere to practise something
difficult, and to fall off and get back up again. Towns near ours have
built them. Ask their councillors whether they regret it.
Some of you are worried about noise, and some of you are worried about
cost. Those are fair concerns, and a group of us has already met the
leisure centre manager to talk about opening hours and fundraising.
We are not asking you to solve every problem young people face. We are
asking for one place that is ours. Please vote yes. Thank you for
listening.

texts.title: The Saturday litter pick
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A short report for a community newsletter.
lines: Last Saturday, more than 40 volunteers met at the park gates for our
spring litter pick. Although the forecast had promised rain, the sky
stayed clear until lunchtime.
Mr Hussain, who has organised the event for 6 years, handed out gloves,
bags, grabbers and hi-vis vests. The youngest volunteer, Maisie, was 7.
The oldest was 82.
By midday we had filled 63 bags. Most of the rubbish was plastic, but we
also found a shopping trolley, a bicycle wheel, a garden gnome and a
single wellington boot.
When the rain finally arrived, we sheltered in the café. Tea was free,
thanks to the owner, and the cakes disappeared in minutes.
Several volunteers said afterwards that the best part of the day was
meeting neighbours they had never spoken to before. One family has
already offered to adopt the stretch of path by the pond.
The next litter pick is on 14 June. Everyone is welcome, and you do not
need to bring anything except yourself.

texts.title: The bakery on Station Road
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A short local-history article.
lines: For 50 years, Hartley’s Bakery has stood on the corner of Station Road.
It’s easy to walk past without noticing it, but the smell of its bread
has been part of the town’s mornings for longer than most of us can
remember.
The shop’s owner, Joan Hartley, took over from her parents in 1998. Her
parents’ recipes are still written in a notebook behind the counter, and
she won’t let anyone photograph them.
The bakery has changed with the times. Its window now shows sourdough
loaves beside the iced buns, and the children’s favourite, a gingerbread
train, has its own shelf. The staff’s uniforms are new, but the ovens
are the same ones her father bought.
Joan’s day starts at 4am. By the time the town’s first commuters walk
past, the shelves are full and the window has steamed up. Regulars know
that the cheese scones have usually gone by 9.
“We’ve had offers to sell,” Joan says. “I’ve always said no. Who’d make
the buns?”

texts.title: A day at the maritime museum
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A short review for a school magazine.
lines: The maritime museum is small; it takes about 2 hours to see everything.
That is not a criticism. Its best rooms are the quiet ones.
One exhibit stopped our whole group: a sailor’s letter home, written in
1912, with a pencil sketch of the ship in the margin. The handwriting
grows shakier towards the end (the sea was rough that night, the label
explains) but the last line is steady: “Tell Mother I am well.”
The museum offers 2 kinds of tour: a guided walk with a volunteer, and
an audio guide you can download. The guided walk is better; the
volunteers have stories that no recording could match.
Younger visitors will enjoy the top floor, where you can try on a
diver’s helmet (it is heavier than it looks) and send a message in Morse
code. Older visitors may prefer the gallery of ship models; some of them
took their makers several years to finish.
Our advice is simple: go early, and leave time for the café on the
ground floor, which serves the best hot chocolate on the seafront.

texts.title: Platform 3
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A short story extract.
lines: The train was already 20 minutes late when Nadia found her brother on
the bench at the end of platform 3.
“You could have answered your phone,” she said.
Sami did not look up. “It died.”
“Mum has rung me 6 times.” She sat down beside him. “What happened?”
For a while he watched the empty track. Then he said, “I didn’t get in.
The music course. They sent the email this morning.”
Nadia knew how many evenings he had spent practising in his room with
the door shut, playing the same few bars over and over until the whole
house could hum them.
Nadia opened her mouth, then closed it again. Somewhere down the line a
signal changed from red to green.
“There’s always next year,” she said, and then wished she hadn’t.
Sami shrugged. “That’s what everyone will say.”
“Come on,” she said at last, standing up and holding out her hand.
“Let’s go home.”

texts.title: Student council report
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A formal report written by a student council.
lines: Report to the Head Teacher: the school canteen
In March, the student council carried out a survey of Year 10 and Year
11 students about the canteen. We were pleased that over 200 students
took part.
Most students were happy with the quality of the food. However, the
queue was a common complaint. Students who have a lesson on the far side
of the site said they often have only 15 minutes to eat.
The council has 2 recommendations. Firstly, a second serving point
should be opened on busy days. Secondly, each year group should have a
set time to queue, so that nobody has to wait more than 10 minutes.
Students also asked for more hot options on Fridays and for the water
fountain by the hall to be repaired. These requests were raised by fewer
students, but the council feels they are worth passing on.
Neither of these changes would be expensive. We would be glad to meet
the catering manager to discuss them.

texts.title: Choosing a school trip
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A short article for a school newsletter.
lines: Every summer, Year 10 have to decide whether they would rather visit the
coast or the city. The choice is harder than it sounds, because the
weather can affect the whole day.
Last year, the students who went to the coast lost their chance to go
sailing when the wind picked up. Their teachers were right to cancel it;
a loose sail in a strong wind is dangerous. The city group, meanwhile,
spent a dry afternoon in the science museum, where they could practise
their French on a group of visiting students.
If you’re choosing this year, think about what you want from the day.
There is no wrong answer. Their experience suggests that the coast is
better when the forecast is good, and the city is the safer bet if you
would hate to lose your plans to the weather.
Whichever trip you choose, your form tutor will need your decision by
Friday. Write it on the slip, and don’t lose it: there were 12 missing
slips last year, and their owners nearly lost their places.
Either way, bring a coat. You’re in England.

texts.title: A student’s draft article (with errors)
texts.author: Inkworks Press
texts.source: Written for Inkworks Press. A student-style draft that contains 10 deliberate errors for you to find.
lines: Every town has a place that people remember from there childhood. In
ours, it was the outdoor swimming pool on Beech Road, which closed 3
years ago.
The council said it was to expensive to repair. Their may be some truth
in that. The changing rooms was falling apart and the water was always
freezing, even in August.
But the pool was more than a place to swim, it was where you went on the
first hot day of the year and where you learned to be brave on the high
board.
Now the site is fenced off and the pools empty. Weeds is growing through
the cracks. It effects everyone who walks past, because it reminds them
of what we have lost.
Other towns have found ways to save their pools. Some are run by
volunteers, and some raise money with summer events. Our town could do
the same if people were given the chance to help.
I think the council should of asked the town before they closed it. Its
not too late to listen.

units.title: Reading closely: stated and implied
units.summary: Explicit information is stated in the words of the text. Implicit information is suggested, and you work it out from clues you can still point to.

questions.prompt: Read lines 1 to 10. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Miss Brill decided to wear her fur.
The air was windy.
She took the fur out of its box that afternoon.
She bought the fur that morning.

questions.explanation: Lines 3 and 8 state the first and third facts directly. The air was “motionless” (line 4), and nothing says she bought the fur: she took it out of its box.

questions.prompt: Which of these is stated explicitly about the fur’s nose?
options: It was made of some black composition and was not firm.
It was missing completely.
It had already been mended with sealing-wax.
It was made of glass.
questions.explanation: Lines 12 to 13 say the nose “was of some black composition, wasn’t at all firm”. She only plans to use sealing-wax “when the time came”, so it has not been mended yet.

questions.prompt: Which inference about Miss Brill is best supported by lines 7 to 11?
options: She treats the fur almost like a pet or a friend.
She is planning to sell the fur.
She is embarrassed to wear old clothes.
She dislikes cold weather.
questions.explanation: She calls it “Dear little thing!” and imagines its eyes speaking to her, which is how people talk to a pet. Nothing in these lines supports the other options.

questions.prompt: Choose all the quotations that suggest the fur is old or worn.
options: “shaken out the moth-powder”
“the blue sky powdered with gold”
“rubbed the life back into the dim little eyes”
“It must have had a knock, somehow”
“she had decided on her fur”
questions.explanation: Moth-powder means long storage, and the “dim” eyes and the damaged nose show wear. The sky and her decision tell us nothing about the fur’s age.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘Miss Brill is happy because it says “Oh, how sweet it was”.’
Answer B: ‘Miss Brill seems lonely: she speaks to the fur as if it were a companion, calling it “Little rogue!”, which suggests she has nobody else to be fond of.’
options: Answer A, because it quotes the text directly.
Answer B, because it makes an inference and explains how the quotation supports it.
Answer A, because it is shorter and more certain.
They are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A only repeats what the text says. Answer B reads beneath the surface and links the evidence to the inference, which is what AO1 rewards when a question asks you to interpret.

questions.prompt: A question says: ‘Read again lines 1 to 6.’ Which answer would earn no credit?
options: The air was motionless.
A leaf came drifting down.
She took the fur out of its box that afternoon.
The sky was blue.
questions.explanation: Taking the fur out of its box happens in line 8, outside the lines set. The June 2023 and June 2025 examiner reports both noted answers taken from outside the given lines, which cannot be credited.
questions.misconception: Using details from outside the lines named in the question.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to what it implies.
pairs: “a faint chill, like a chill from a glass of iced water before you sip”
Even on a fine day there is a hint of cold.
She feels tender towards the fur.
“It must have had a knock, somehow.”
“but that came from walking, she supposed”
She explains away a feeling rather than examining it.
questions.explanation: Each quotation states something small, and the implication is what it suggests about the day, the fur or Miss Brill herself.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Miss Brill is sad because the text says “something light and sad”.’ What is the problem with this inference?
options: She corrects herself at once with “no, not sad, exactly”, so the text holds back from the word sad.
The quotation comes from outside the extract.
‘Sad’ is too informal for an exam answer.
There is no problem: the inference is fully supported.
questions.explanation: Reading the whole sentence matters. Miss Brill pushes the word away and replaces it with “something gentle”, which is more interesting: she may be avoiding a feeling she does not want to name.

questions.prompt: What can you infer about Miss Brill from the way she treats her fur in lines 7 to 17? Make 2 inferences and support each with a short quotation.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): Miss Brill is affectionate and perhaps lonely. She calls the fur “Little rogue!” as if it were a cheeky pet, which suggests she has few people to share that warmth with. She is also careful and thrifty: she plans to fix the nose with “a little dab of black sealing-wax” rather than buy a new fur, so she may not have much money.
checklist: Makes 2 different inferences, not 2 versions of the same point
Supports each inference with a short quotation from lines 7 to 17
Explains the link between the quotation and the inference
Uses tentative words such as ‘suggests’ or ‘perhaps’ where the text only hints
questions.explanation: Strong inference answers move from what the words say to what they suggest, and keep the evidence short.

questions.prompt: Using the whole extract, explain what Miss Brill’s thoughts about her fur suggest about her life. Support your ideas with quotations.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): On the surface this is a cheerful outing on a bright afternoon, yet the fur reveals a quieter life. Miss Brill has stored it carefully with “moth-powder” and now rubs “the life back” into it, as if reviving an old companion; the care she gives an object hints that there are few people to give it to. When she imagines the eyes asking “What has been happening to me?”, the question seems to belong to her as much as to the fur. Her habit of explaining things away, the tingling “came from walking, she supposed”, and her refusal of the word “sad” suggest someone who keeps unwelcome feelings at a distance. The fur is shabby but treasured, and she may be too.
checklist: Builds an overall interpretation, not a list of separate facts
Selects precise quotations from across the extract
Explains how small details (the moth-powder, the dim eyes) hint at something larger
Notices where Miss Brill avoids or corrects her own feelings
Keeps inferences tied to the text rather than guessing beyond it
questions.explanation: The best answers notice that the fur and its owner are described in similar ways, and explain how that hints at Miss Brill’s situation without overstating it.

units.title: Choosing and using quotations
units.summary: Quote the fewest words that prove your point and fit them into your own sentence. Short quotations let you zoom in on the word that matters.

questions.prompt: What is the best length for most quotations in a language answer?
options: A single word or a short phrase
A whole sentence every time
A whole paragraph
As long as possible, to show you have read it
questions.explanation: Short quotations point straight at the word doing the work, and leave you time to explain it.

questions.prompt: Which quotation best shows that the weather was perfect?
options: “the sky without a cloud”
“the men came to put up the marquee”
“She had washed her hair before breakfast”
“Where do you want the marquee put, mother?”
questions.explanation: “the sky without a cloud” (line 3) is about the weather. The others are about the party preparations or Meg.

questions.prompt: A student wants to write about how the roses are made to seem almost holy. Which quotation is most precise?
options: “visited by archangels”
“Hundreds, yes, literally hundreds, had come out in a single night; the green bushes bowed down as though they had been visited by archangels”
“As for the roses”
“the only flowers that impress people at garden-parties”
questions.explanation: The idea of holiness lives in “archangels”. The long version buries that word, and the other options say nothing about holiness.

questions.prompt: Is each quotation embedded so that the student’s sentence makes sense?

statements.s: ‘The roses seem to have been “visited by archangels”, as if blessed.’
‘The gardener had worked “since dawn”, so the family’s perfect lawn depends on someone else’s labour.’
‘The sky is perfect because “Windless, warm, the sky without a cloud.” shows.’
‘Meg sits with “a dark wet curl stamped on each cheek”, still not ready for the day.’

questions.explanation: An embedded quotation reads as part of your own grammatical sentence. The third sentence breaks down because the quotation is dropped in without being fitted to the words around it.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘The mother says “My dear child, it’s no use asking me. I’m determined to leave everything to you children this year. Forget I am your mother. Treat me as an honoured guest.” This shows she is relaxed.’
Answer B: ‘The mother asks to be treated as “an honoured guest”, a playful swap of roles that hands the work to her children while keeping her importance.’
options: Answer A, because it gives the full speech.
Answer B, because the short quotation lets the student comment on precise words.
Answer A, because ‘relaxed’ is a clear point.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A’s quotation is so long that the comment cannot point at anything. Answer B picks “an honoured guest” and explains what the phrase suggests about her.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The phrase “the green bushes bowed down as though they had been visited by archangels” shows the bushes were heavy.’ What would an examiner most likely say?
options: The quotation is too long to be called a phrase, and the comment ignores the key word ‘archangels’.
Quotations must always be whole sentences.
Bushes are not worth analysing.
Nothing: this is a top-level comment.
questions.explanation: The June 2023 Paper 1 examiner report noted very long quotations introduced as ‘the phrase’, which left students with nothing precise to say. Choose the word that carries the meaning and explain it.
questions.misconception: Quoting a long chunk and calling it ‘the phrase’, then commenting only on the obvious meaning.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for using a quotation in a sensible order.
items: Decide what point you want to make about the question focus
Find the shortest quotation that proves it
Embed it in your own sentence
Zoom in on a key word and explain its effect
questions.explanation: Start from your point, not from a quotation you happen to like. Then keep it short, fit it in and explain it.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences misquotes the text?
options: ‘The lawns had been swept until even the dark rosettes “seemed to shine”.’
‘The blue sky was “veiled with a haze of light gold”.’
‘The roses had come out “in a single day”.’
‘The mother tells the children to “Forget I am your mother.”’
questions.explanation: The text says the roses came out “in a single night” (line 10). A misquotation can change the meaning, and examiners cannot credit words that are not in the source.
questions.misconception: Misremembering or miscopying a quotation.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite this weak sentence so that it uses a short, embedded quotation and comments on a key word:
‘The writer says “They could not have had a more perfect day for a garden-party if they had ordered it.” This shows it was a nice day.’
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The weather is so perfect that it could have been “ordered”, as if this family is used to getting whatever it asks for, even from the sky.
checklist: Uses a quotation of only a few words
Fits the quotation into a grammatical sentence of your own
Comments on what a key word (such as “ordered”) suggests
Goes beyond ‘nice’ to say something about the family or the mood
questions.explanation: One word, “ordered”, carries a hint about the family’s privilege. Picking it out turns a description into analysis.

questions.prompt: How does Mansfield present the family’s comfortable, privileged world in lines 1 to 19? Use at least 4 short, embedded quotations.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Mansfield makes the family’s world seem so smooth that even nature obeys it. The day is so ideal it might have been “ordered”, and the roses seem to understand that they must “impress people”, as though flowers too know their place at a garden-party. Behind this ease is other people’s work: the gardener has been busy “since dawn”, and “the men” arrive to put up the marquee before breakfast is over. The mother’s wish to be treated as “an honoured guest” turns responsibility into a game, while Meg, with “a dark wet curl stamped on each cheek”, is far too comfortable to supervise anyone. The quotations together suggest a family that is charming but rarely has to lift a finger.
checklist: Makes a clear overall point about privilege or comfort
Uses several short quotations, fitted into its own sentences
Comments on the connotations of chosen words
Notices the contrast between the family and the people working for them
Covers the extract as a whole, not only the first few lines
questions.explanation: Short embedded quotations let you build a whole argument about the family while keeping the focus on the writer’s words.

units.title: Explaining effects: how and why
units.summary: Naming a technique earns little on its own. Explain why the writer chose these words and what they make the reader think, feel or picture.

questions.prompt: What earns most credit in an answer about language?
options: Explaining why the writer chose particular words and what they suggest
Naming as many techniques as possible
Retelling what happens
Saying the text makes the reader want to read on
questions.explanation: Mark schemes reward the explanation of effects. A technique name is only useful if it helps you explain.

questions.prompt: Match each word from the text to its connotations.
pairs: moving fast and smoothly, like a rolling ball
a sudden, sharp feeling of pain or longing
something thin and delicate, easily lost
questions.explanation: Connotations are the associations a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning. They are the raw material for explaining effect.

questions.prompt: “past waltzing lamp-posts” (line 6). What is the main effect of the word ‘waltzing’?
options: Leila’s excitement makes even the street seem to dance, as if the ball has already begun.
The lamp-posts are falling over.
It shows the driver is reckless.
It tells us the ball has finished.
questions.explanation: The opening says it was hard to say exactly when the ball began; the dancing lamp-posts show that in Leila’s mind it started in the cab.

questions.prompt: Complete the method: Pick a word, picture it, ___ it with a plainer word, then connect it to the question.
questions.explanation: Comparing the writer’s word with a plainer one shows what the chosen word adds. That difference is the effect.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘The writer uses a simile, “like a flower through snow”, to create a vivid image for the reader.’
Answer B: ‘Laura’s dark head “pushing” above her white fur is compared to a flower breaking through snow, so Leila sees her cousin as fresh and full of life. Everything looks magical to her tonight.’
options: Answer A, because it names the technique correctly.
Answer B, because it explains what the image suggests about Laura and about Leila’s mood.
Answer A, because ‘vivid image’ is a technical phrase.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: ‘Creates a vivid image’ could be said about almost any image. Answer B explains what this particular image suggests.

questions.prompt: Which comment on “every single thing was so new and exciting” (lines 12 to 13) is too general to earn much credit?
options: ‘It makes the reader want to read on.’
‘“every single thing” stretches her excitement to tiny details, so nothing is too small to thrill her.’
‘“so new” reminds us this is her first ball, which is why she cannot act bored.’
‘The list that follows shows her eyes darting from one lovely detail to the next.’
questions.explanation: The June 2025 Paper 1 examiner report described ‘makes the reader want to read on’ as a Level 1 comment. It could be said of any text, so it shows no understanding of this one.
questions.misconception: Using a stock comment such as ‘makes the reader want to read on’ instead of explaining an effect.

questions.prompt: Which comments explain an effect, rather than only naming a feature? Choose all that apply.
options: ‘The writer uses a semicolon.’
‘“tried not to care” shows Leila forcing herself to copy the others’ calm, which only makes her eagerness clearer.’
‘There is a list in line 13.’
‘Wanting to keep the tissue paper “as a keepsake” shows she wants to hold on to every scrap of the night.’
‘This is personification.’
questions.explanation: Only the second and fourth comments say what the words do. The others name a feature and stop.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The bolster is personified because it turns into a young man.’ What is wrong with this?
options: The bolster only “felt like the sleeve of an unknown young man’s dress suit”: it is a simile, and nothing turns into a man.
‘Bolster’ is a verb.
Nothing: the comment is correct.
Personification can only describe animals.
questions.explanation: The examiner reports for June 2022 and June 2024 both warned against forcing labels that do not apply. Read the comparison carefully: Leila imagines the cushion as a partner’s sleeve.
questions.misconception: Forcing a technique label onto a phrase it does not fit.

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of the phrase “the sleeve of an unknown young man’s dress suit” (line 5). Use the method: pick, picture, compare, connect.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Instead of saying the bolster was soft, Mansfield has Leila feel it as “the sleeve” of a stranger’s evening suit, so an ordinary cab cushion becomes her first dance partner. The word “unknown” matters: Leila has no particular young man in mind, only the thrilling idea of one, which shows how innocent and full of expectation she is.
checklist: Picks out a key word such as “unknown” or “sleeve”
Explains what Leila imagines and why
Compares the image with a plainer description
Connects the effect to Leila’s excitement or innocence
questions.explanation: The best answers notice that the partner is “unknown”, so the excitement is about the idea of a ball rather than a real person.

questions.prompt: How does the writer use language to show Leila’s excitement in lines 1 to 18?
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Mansfield lets Leila’s excitement spill over onto everything she touches. The ball starts before it begins: the cab is her “first real partner” and the lamp-posts are “waltzing”, so the whole street seems to join the dance. Her attempt to be calm is shown through repetition, “she tried not to smile too much; she tried not to care”, and the effort behind those words gives her away. When the narrative lists “Meg’s tuberoses, Jose’s long loop of amber” it follows her eyes darting from detail to detail, each one precious. Even rubbish becomes treasure: the tissue paper gives her “a pang”, a word of almost painful longing, because she wants to keep it “as a keepsake”. The language makes her joy touching because it is so intense and so unguarded.
checklist: Analyses the effect of individual word choices
Chooses short, precise quotations from across the extract
Uses terms such as repetition or list accurately and only when helpful
Explains how the language shows excitement, not just that it does
Builds a clear overall view of Leila
questions.explanation: Top answers explain how each choice shows excitement and link the details into an overall picture of Leila.

units.title: Language terms (1): words and images
units.summary: Terms such as simile, metaphor and personification are tools. Use a term when it sharpens your explanation, then say what the words do.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: giving human qualities to something that is not human
an association a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning
questions.explanation: These terms appear often in AQA mark schemes, but they only earn credit when they support an explanation of effect.

questions.prompt: “like the stalk of a huge black mushroom” (lines 8 to 9) is an example of:
options: a simile
a metaphor
personification
onomatopoeia
questions.explanation: It compares the wood-pile to a mushroom stalk using ‘like’, so it is a simile.

questions.prompt: Which quotation uses personification?
options: “it seemed afraid to unfurl its timid, quivering light”
“a beautiful night, mild, starry”
“quick, nervous strides”
“strapped into a neat sausage”
questions.explanation: A lantern cannot feel afraid or timid, so the writer gives it human feelings. ‘Nervous strides’ describes a real person.

questions.prompt: Choose all the quotations that belong to a semantic field of darkness.
options: “solid darkness”
“all that blackness”
“crackling black ulster”
“mild, starry”
“white woolly shawl”
questions.explanation: A semantic field is a group of words linked by meaning. The words linked to darkness build the gloom of the wharf; ‘starry’ and ‘white’ point the other way.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘The umbrella is personified. This is effective.’
Answer B: ‘The swan’s-head handle gives Fenella “a sharp little peck”, as if even the umbrella is nagging her to keep up, which adds to the sense of hurry around her.’
options: Answer A, because it uses the correct term.
Answer B, because it explains what the image adds to the scene.
Answer A, because it is concise.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: ‘Effective’ tells the examiner nothing. Answer B explains how the image works and links it to the hurry of the scene.

questions.prompt: A student calls “angrily” (line 21) an adjective. Which is correct?
options: It is an adverb: it describes how the boy was jerked along.
It is an adjective describing the boy.
It is a noun.
It is a metaphor.
questions.explanation: The June 2025 Paper 1 examiner report noted students confusing adverbs and adjectives. Adverbs tell us how an action is done; here it is the jerking that is angry.
questions.misconception: Confusing adverbs with adjectives.

questions.prompt: Match each image to its effect.
pairs: The dark seems so thick it is like stone.
“a baby fly that had fallen into the cream”
The boy looks tiny and helpless.
A homely, childlike picture of tightly rolled luggage.
Her father is anxious and in a hurry.
questions.explanation: Each image does a different job. Matching image to effect is the step that turns a term into analysis.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The writer uses a metaphor: “he looked like a baby fly”.’ What is the error?
options: It is a simile, because the comparison uses ‘like’.
It is onomatopoeia.
‘Fly’ is a verb here.
There is no error.
questions.explanation: A metaphor says one thing is another; a simile uses ‘like’ or ‘as’. Getting the term wrong weakens an otherwise sensible point.

questions.prompt: Explain how the writer uses personification in lines 7 to 11 to create atmosphere.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The lantern “seemed afraid to unfurl its timid, quivering light”, so even the only source of light on the wharf is frightened of the dark. Words such as “timid” and “quivering” make the light seem small and trembling, and the verb “unfurl” suggests something that wants to open out but does not dare. The darkness therefore feels huge and powerful, and the scene becomes slightly threatening from a child’s point of view.
checklist: Identifies the personification accurately
Picks out individual words such as “afraid”, “timid” or “quivering”
Explains what the personification suggests about the light and the darkness
Links the effect to the atmosphere of the scene
questions.explanation: Personification earns marks when you explain what giving human feelings to the lantern does to the mood.

questions.prompt: How does the writer use language to describe the wharf at night in lines 1 to 11?
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Mansfield builds the wharf as a place swallowed by darkness. The repetition in “It was dark on the Old Wharf, very dark” stresses the gloom, and the list of “wool sheds, the cattle trucks, the cranes” shows everyday objects turned into shapes “carved out of solid darkness”, as though the dark were heavy enough to sculpt. The simile of the wood-pile as “the stalk of a huge black mushroom” makes the setting strange and slightly unreal, like a fairy tale seen by a child. Against all this, the lantern is personified as “afraid” and “timid”, so the one light is weak and shrinking. The language creates a mood that is mysterious rather than simply frightening, and it prepares us to see the voyage through Fenella’s eyes.
checklist: Analyses the effects of specific words and images
Uses terms such as simile, personification and repetition accurately
Selects precise, short quotations from lines 1 to 11
Explains how the language builds a mood or atmosphere
Connects the description to a viewpoint or overall effect
questions.explanation: The strongest answers explain how several images work together to build the atmosphere, using terms precisely.

units.title: Language terms (2): sound and sentences
units.summary: Sound patterns and sentence forms matter only when you can explain what they do at that exact point in the text.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: repeated sounds at the start of nearby words
a word that sounds like its meaning
a sentence with one main clause
a main clause with at least 1 subordinate clause
questions.explanation: These are the sound and sentence terms you are most likely to use. Learn the exact meaning so you use them accurately.

questions.prompt: “She winked quickly.” (line 7) is:
options: a simple sentence
a complex sentence
a compound sentence
a minor sentence
questions.explanation: It has one main clause (subject ‘She’, verb ‘winked’) and nothing else, so it is a simple sentence.

questions.prompt: Lines 8 to 9 read: “The mast was straight; the waves were regular; the lighthouse was upright; but the blot had spread.” What is the effect of the final clause?
options: After a list of things returning to normal, ‘but’ turns to the one thing that cannot be undone.
It shows the weather is improving.
It simply makes the list longer.
It introduces a new character.
questions.explanation: The semicolons line up signs that her tears have cleared. The last clause breaks the pattern: the ink blot, like her grief, has already spread.

questions.prompt: Choose all the phrases that use alliteration.
options: “stray solitary”
“gleaning a few golden straws”
“pale blue ink”
“the lighthouse wobbled”
“herrings in a barrel”
questions.explanation: ‘stray solitary’ repeats the s sound and ‘gleaning … golden’ repeats the g sound. The other phrases have no repeated opening sounds.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘The writer uses short sentences to build tension.’
Answer B: ‘The short sentences “She winked quickly. Accidents were awful things. She winked again.” copy Betty’s blinks as she tries to clear her tears, and the blunt thought in the middle hints at the grief she is pushing away.’
options: Answer A, because it names the sentence type.
Answer B, because it explains what these particular sentences do at this point.
Answer A, because tension is always the effect of short sentences.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A could be written about any text. Answer B ties the sentence form to Betty’s actions and feelings in this moment.

questions.prompt: Which advice about commenting on sentence forms matches what examiners have said?
options: Only comment on a sentence form if you can explain what it does at that particular point.
Every answer must mention a short sentence.
Long sentences always show calm.
