Short sentences always create tension.
questions.explanation: The June 2019 Paper 1 examiner report found comments on sentence length less successful than work on words and phrases, and the June 2023 Paper 2 report described students picking short sentences and then having nothing to say.
questions.misconception: Believing a sentence form always has the same effect, such as ‘short sentences create tension’.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to the feature it shows.
pairs: a question with capital letters for stress
“packed though we are like herrings in a barrel”
questions.explanation: Identifying the feature is the first step. Each of these also needs an explanation of its effect in a full answer.

questions.prompt: Lines 22 to 23 read: “Scarborough is seven hundred miles from Cornwall: Captain Barfoot is in Scarborough: Seabrook is dead.” A student says the colons introduce a list of Betty’s possessions. What is wrong?
options: The colons link blunt facts that build towards Seabrook’s death; there are no possessions.
There are no colons in these lines.
Colons are only used before quotations.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: Each colon pushes the reader to the next fact, and the last one lands on the death of Betty’s husband. Misreading punctuation leads to a comment that does not fit the text.

questions.prompt: Lines 23 to 30 (from “Tears made all the dahlias”) form one long sentence. Explain the effect of this sentence structure.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The sentence keeps adding clauses joined by “and”: the tears make the dahlias “undulate”, then flash the glass house, then spangle the kitchen, then reach into Mrs Jarvis’s thoughts at church. The structure spreads outwards like the ink blot, so Betty’s grief seems to soak into every part of her life. It ends on the list “lonely, unprotected, poor creatures”, which slows the rhythm, and then a short plain sentence states that she has been a widow for 2 years, bringing us down to the fact behind it all.
checklist: Identifies the long sentence and how it is built (clauses joined by ‘and’)
Explains how the structure mirrors the spreading of Betty’s grief
Comments on the list and the short sentence that follows
Uses short quotations to support each point
questions.explanation: Sentence forms earn credit when you connect the shape of the sentence to the meaning at that point.

questions.prompt: How does the writer use sound and sentence forms to show Betty Flanders’s feelings in lines 1 to 30?
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Woolf uses sentence forms to show grief breaking through ordinary tasks. Betty’s letter keeps stopping: “nothing for it but to leave” is repeated as she rereads it, as if she is stuck on the words. Short sentences such as “She winked again.” show her trying to blink away tears, while semicolons build a calm list, “The mast was straight; the waves were regular”, that is undone by “but the blot had spread”. Later, colons force together blunt facts until we reach “Seabrook is dead.”, a sentence so short it feels like a blow. Sound adds to this: the soft s sounds of “widows stray solitary” make the image quiet and lonely. Sentence shape and sound together let us feel a sorrow that Betty herself does not put into words.
checklist: Analyses how specific sentence forms create effects at particular points
Comments on sound (such as sibilance or alliteration) with a clear purpose
Uses accurate terminology throughout
Supports points with short, precise quotations
Links the methods to Betty’s hidden feelings
questions.explanation: Top answers show how form and sound reveal feelings that the character does not state, using terms accurately.

units.title: Structure terms you need
units.summary: Structure is how a text is arranged: where it starts, how its focus moves and where it ends. Language is about words; structure is about order and shape.

questions.prompt: Match each structural term to its meaning.
pairs: attention moves from one thing or person to another
a moment where the direction or mood changes
the ending returns to the opening
questions.explanation: These are structural terms that AQA mark schemes list. They describe how parts of a text relate, not individual words.

questions.prompt: The extract opens with a single sentence in a paragraph of its own (line 1). What does this do as an opening?
options: It sets up a simple, everyday task that the rest of the extract grows from.
It describes the setting in detail.
It is the climax of the extract.
It is a flashback.
questions.explanation: Buying flowers is ordinary, and the plain sentence gives the reader a clear starting point before the narrative moves into memory.

questions.prompt: At which point does the narrative move back in time to Clarissa’s youth?
options: “For so it had always seemed to her” (line 5)
“The doors would be taken off their hinges” (lines 2 to 3)
“She stiffened a little on the kerb” (line 22)
“A charming woman, Scrope Purvis thought her” (line 23)
questions.explanation: From line 5 Clarissa recalls opening the French windows at Bourton when she was 18. The other lines are set in the present.

questions.prompt: Put these in the order they appear in the extract.
items: Clarissa decides to buy the flowers
Clarissa remembers opening the windows at Bourton
Peter Walsh’s remark about vegetables is recalled
Clarissa waits on the kerb
Scrope Purvis watches her
questions.explanation: The extract moves from the present into memory, then returns to the street, where the focus shifts to a neighbour.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘In line 22 the writer starts a new paragraph.’
Answer B: ‘At line 23 the focus shifts from Clarissa’s memories to how a neighbour sees her, “A charming woman”, so after being deep inside her thoughts we suddenly view her from outside, a small, upright figure on the kerb.’
options: Answer A, because it gives a line number.
Answer B, because it explains what the shift does to our view of Clarissa.
Answer A, because paragraphs are a structural feature.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Spotting a new paragraph is not enough. Answer B explains the shift in perspective and its effect.

questions.prompt: Which comment is about structure rather than language?
options: ‘The simile “like the flap of a wave” makes the air sound refreshing.’
‘The narrative moves from London back to Bourton and then returns to the kerb, so the past keeps breaking into the present.’
‘“plunged” is a strong verb.’
‘“squeak” is onomatopoeia.’
questions.explanation: The June 2022 Paper 1 examiner report noted students writing about language features in the structure question. Only the second comment is about how the text is arranged.
questions.misconception: Writing about language features when the question asks about structure.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the structure is true or false.

statements.s: The whole extract is seen only through Clarissa’s eyes.
A sound in the present sets off Clarissa’s memory of Bourton.
The extract ends with a flashback.
Peter Walsh is introduced through a memory rather than in person.

questions.explanation: Scrope Purvis’s view breaks in at the end, which is set in the present. The squeak of the hinges “which she could hear now” links past and present.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The structure is chronological: events are told in the order they happened.’ Why is this wrong?
options: The narrative jumps back more than 30 years to Bourton, then returns to the present.
There are no events in the extract.
The extract is told backwards from the end.
It is not wrong.
questions.explanation: Clarissa was 18 at Bourton and is now over 50, so the memory reaches back decades before returning to the street.

questions.prompt: Explain why the writer might have placed Scrope Purvis’s view of Clarissa (lines 23 to 27) straight after her memories.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): After lines full of Clarissa’s rushing thoughts, the focus suddenly moves outside her to a neighbour who sees “a charming woman” perched like a bird on the kerb. The shift reminds us that the rich inner world we have just shared is invisible to others: to him she is “very upright” and composed. Placing the outside view straight after the memories sharpens the contrast between how she feels and how she appears.
checklist: Identifies the shift in perspective
Explains the contrast between Clarissa’s inner thoughts and the outside view
Comments on why this comes at this point
Supports points with short references
questions.explanation: Structure questions reward explaining why something comes where it does, not only what it is.

questions.prompt: How has the writer structured this extract to move between past and present? Use structural terms in your answer.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The extract opens in the present with a single plain sentence about flowers, giving a firm foothold before Woolf lets memory take over. A sensory link, the hinge’s “little squeak … which she could hear now”, triggers a flashback to Bourton, and for most of the extract the past dominates, ending on Peter Walsh’s half-remembered sayings. The narrative then snaps back to the present with “She stiffened a little on the kerb”, a pivotal point where we return to the street. Finally the focus shifts to Scrope Purvis, who sees only her outside. The structure moves inward and then outward, showing how the past lives inside Clarissa while to others she is simply a woman waiting to cross.
checklist: Tracks how the text moves between present and past
Uses terms such as flashback, shift in focus and pivotal point accurately
Explains the effect of each structural choice
Refers to precise points in the text
Comments on the extract as a whole, including its ending
questions.explanation: The best structure answers follow the whole text, using terms precisely and explaining each move.

units.title: Words for tone and perspective
units.summary: Tone is the attitude a writer’s words convey. Describe it with precise words such as wry, sombre or sympathetic, never just ‘positive’ or ‘negative’.

questions.prompt: Which word best describes the tone of lines 1 to 12?
options: bleak
joyful
furious
excited
questions.explanation: Phrases such as “the stillness of death” and “cold and lifeless” make the empty streets bleak and desolate.

questions.prompt: Match each tone word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Precise tone words let you describe an attitude exactly, which examiners reward on Paper 2 Question 4.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s tone when describing the cat in lines 15 to 19?
options: playfully mocking, as if the cat were a man sneaking home after a night out
frightened
angry
sorrowful
questions.explanation: The cat worries about his “character” and his “gallantry of the preceding night”, words that belong to a person with a reputation. The mock-serious tone is comic.

questions.prompt: Choose all the quotations that show sympathy for poor people.
options: “to dream of food and warmth”
“coiled up his chilly limbs”
“a rakish-looking cat”
“The coach-stands in the larger thoroughfares are deserted”
questions.explanation: The homeless man curled up in the cold, dreaming of food, is described gently. The cat and the coach-stands are not about poverty.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘The writer’s perspective is negative about London.’
Answer B: ‘Dickens writes as a fascinated observer: he finds the empty streets eerie, with “the stillness of death”, yet he enjoys the comedy of the cat’s “caution and slyness”, so his perspective mixes unease with amusement.’
options: Answer A, because it gives a clear opinion.
Answer B, because it uses precise words for attitude and supports them.
Answer A, because perspectives are always positive or negative.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer B captures a mixed attitude in precise words and backs each part with evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is ‘The writer is negative about the streets’ a weak way to describe his perspective?
options: It is too general; a precise word such as ‘uneasy’ or ‘amused’, explained with evidence, shows clearer understanding.
Writers never hold negative views.
It should say ‘positive’ instead.
Perspective should never be described in an answer.
questions.explanation: The June 2022 Paper 2 examiner report called ‘positive versus negative’ a Level 1 generalisation, and the June 2023 report asked for more precise vocabulary for perspectives, such as sceptical or enthralled.
questions.misconception: Describing a writer’s perspective only as ‘positive’ or ‘negative’.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to the tone it creates.
pairs: “the stillness of death is over the streets”
“as if he were conscious that his character depended on his gallantry”
“listlessly gazing on the deserted prospect before him”
questions.explanation: One extract can hold several tones. Tracking how the tone changes is a strong way to write about perspective.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Dickens hates the cat, because he calls it “rakish-looking”.’ What is the problem?
options: The description is affectionate and comic: ‘rakish’ makes the cat a charming rogue, so ‘hates’ misreads the tone.
‘rakish-looking’ is not in the text.
Animals cannot be described in a perspective answer.
There is no problem.
questions.explanation: Comic or ironic description is easy to take literally. The June 2024 Paper 2 examiner report noted students taking sarcastic or exaggerated comments at face value.

questions.prompt: Choose 2 precise words to describe the writer’s attitude in lines 1 to 12. Support each with a quotation.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): Dickens is uneasy: he says “the stillness of death is over the streets”, which makes the city seem like a corpse rather than a sleeping town. He is also sympathetic to the poor, because the homeless man has curled up “to dream of food and warmth”, a gentle phrase that asks us to imagine his hunger.
checklist: Uses 2 precise attitude words (for example uneasy, sympathetic, disapproving)
Supports each word with a short quotation
Explains how the quotation shows that attitude
Avoids ‘positive’ and ‘negative’
questions.explanation: Precise attitude words, each backed by evidence, show a clear understanding of perspective.

questions.prompt: How does the writer convey his perspective on London before sunrise in lines 1 to 24?
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Dickens presents the hour before dawn as a strange pause in the city’s life, and his attitude shifts from sombre to wryly amused. The opening sentences sweep away the night’s drunkards and the “wretched”, and leave “the stillness of death”, so the empty streets feel eerie and almost lifeless. His sympathy shows in the image of the vagrant dreaming “of food and warmth”. Then the tone lightens: a policeman gazes “listlessly” and a cat creeps home with the guilty “caution and slyness” of a man after a night out, described with mock seriousness. The perspective is that of a curious observer who finds the sleeping city both melancholy and comic.
checklist: Describes the perspective with precise words
Shows how the tone changes across the extract
Explains the methods that convey the attitude (word choice, imagery, contrast)
Uses well-chosen quotations from across the extract
Builds an overall view of the writer’s attitude
questions.explanation: Top answers show a mixed or changing perspective and explain how the writer’s methods convey it.

units.title: Big ideas and context: use with care
units.summary: Big ideas grow out of details in the text. Context helps only when it explains something in the passage; bolted-on history earns little.

questions.prompt: Which big idea does this extract explore most clearly?
options: a childhood lost to work and poverty
the fun of city life
the history of watercress farming
friendship between children
questions.explanation: The girl has “entirely lost all childish ways” (line 2), and every detail builds that idea.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about using context is true or false.

statements.s: On Paper 1, long paragraphs of historical background earn extra marks.
A brief point about when a text was written can help if it explains something in the text.
Big ideas should grow out of details in the text.
You should learn a context paragraph and add it to every answer.

questions.explanation: Context is useful only when it sheds light on the passage. Examiners have repeatedly noted that general background is not credited for its own sake.

questions.prompt: Which detail most clearly shows that the girl has missed out on play?
options: “the look of amazement that answered me”
“where she lived”
“Farringdon-market”
“some hot dinner”
questions.explanation: When Mayhew asks about toys and games, she looks amazed, as if these things are foreign to her.

questions.prompt: Choose all the quotations that show the girl’s world is very small.
options: “All her knowledge seemed to begin and end with water-cresses”
“She knew no more of London than that part she had seen on her rounds”
“The parks!”
“calm earnestness”
“I did not know how to talk with her”
questions.explanation: Her knowledge stops at watercress and her rounds, and she has never heard of the parks. The other quotations are about her manner or Mayhew’s difficulty.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘This shows Victorian England was a terrible place for poor people, because the rich ignored the poor and there were workhouses everywhere.’
Answer B: ‘Mayhew presents a childhood that has been stolen: the girl meets talk of toys with “amazement”, and her face is “wrinkled where the dimples ought to have been”, as if work has aged her too soon.’
options: Answer A, because it shows knowledge of history.
Answer B, because its big idea grows from precise details in the text.
Answer A, because it covers society as a whole.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A makes sweeping claims that the extract does not mention. Answer B builds its big idea from the writer’s words.

questions.prompt: A student spends half an answer explaining Victorian laws on child labour before mentioning the extract. What would examiners say?
options: Context that is not tied to the text earns little; the focus must be how the writer presents the girl.
This is the best way to reach the top level.
Context should always come first and be as long as possible.
Laws are the main focus of Paper 2.
questions.explanation: The June 2024 Paper 1 examiner report noted long passages of assumed context that could not be credited, and the June 2024 Paper 2 report warned against bolted-on claims about class or gender not rooted in the text.
questions.misconception: Bolting on historical context instead of analysing the text.

questions.prompt: Match each detail to the big idea it supports.
pairs: “wrinkled where the dimples ought to have been”
“Would they let such as me go there”
feeling shut out of a world others enjoy
“she wasn’t used to meat, only on a Sunday”
“I did not know how to talk with her”
the gap between the writer’s world and hers
questions.explanation: A big idea should always be anchored to a detail, so you can show the examiner where it comes from.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Mayhew thinks the girl is ungrateful, because she refuses a hot dinner.’ What is wrong?
options: She refuses because rich food “made her sick” when she was not used to it; Mayhew presents this with pity, as a sign of hunger.
She accepts the dinner happily.
The dinner is not mentioned in the extract.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: Read the reason given in lines 25 to 26. The detail shows how little she usually eats, which is the opposite of ingratitude.

questions.prompt: Explain how 1 detail in the extract links to a bigger idea about childhood.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): When Mayhew describes the parks, the girl asks, “Would they let such as me go there”. The phrase “such as me” shows she already sees herself as a different, lesser kind of person, shut out of places where “children played”. This links to the big idea that poverty has taken away not only her play but her sense that she belongs in the world other children enjoy.
checklist: Chooses a precise detail and quotes it
Explains what the detail shows about the girl
Links the detail to a wider idea about childhood
Keeps the big idea rooted in the text rather than in general history
questions.explanation: The skill is moving from a small detail to a large idea while keeping the text in view.

questions.prompt: ‘Mayhew wants his readers to feel pity, and also to feel uncomfortable.’ How far do you agree? Refer closely to the extract.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): I largely agree. Pity is clear from the start: Mayhew calls the scene “cruelly pathetic” and describes an “infant” speaking of “the bitterest struggles of life”, so the reader is moved by the mismatch between her age and her experience. Yet he also makes us uncomfortable by showing his own failure: “I did not know how to talk with her”, and his attempts at toys and games meet only “amazement”. His comfortable world, and by implication the reader’s, has nothing to offer her. The final detail, that she is used to meat “only on a Sunday”, closes the paragraph on a plain fact rather than a comment, leaving readers to sit with what it means. The extract therefore moves from sympathy towards an uneasy recognition of the gap between the classes.
checklist: States a clear view on the statement
Evaluates how the writer creates pity and discomfort
Comments on methods such as word choice, the writer’s own reactions and placing of details
Uses precise quotations from across the extract
Develops an interpretation without relying on bolted-on context
questions.explanation: Strong evaluation keeps returning to the writer’s methods and uses the text, not general history, as evidence.

units.title: Question 1: multiple choice on the opening
units.summary: Paper 1 Question 1 is now 4 multiple-choice questions on the opening lines, 1 mark each, with 3 options. Answer only from the lines named, and choose what the text says, not what seems likely.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 1 to 7. Why is it better not to walk arm-in-arm in these streets?
options: The streets are very narrow.
The streets are dangerous at night.
It is against the law.
questions.explanation: Lines 1 to 2 say the streets “are very narrow, it is better not to walk down them arm-in-arm”.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 1 to 7. Who will have to make “flying leaps into the mud”?
options: lawyers’ clerks
young lady typists
small boys
questions.explanation: Line 3 names the lawyers’ clerks. The typists are mentioned next, but they only “fidget behind you”, a tempting distractor.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 1 to 7. According to the writer, what must eccentricity do in these streets?
options: pay the penalty
hide behind a cloak
keep to the edge of the pavement
questions.explanation: Line 5: “eccentricity must pay the penalty”. The cloak and the pavement edge appear later, describing Mrs Ambrose and her husband.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 8 to 10. In which month does the scene take place? Type 1 word.
questions.explanation: Line 8: “One afternoon in the beginning of October”. Retrieval answers must come from the lines named, so check the exact words.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Student A and Student B explain how they answered ‘Why do people stare at the couple?’
Student A: ‘I picked the option that sounded most dramatic.’
Student B: ‘I found the lines about the stare and checked which option matched “the unfriendly stare which was bestowed upon Mr. Ambrose’s height and upon Mrs. Ambrose’s cloak”.’
options: Student A, because exam answers are often dramatic.
Student B, because the answer is checked against the exact words in the lines.
Student A, because it is quicker.
Both methods are equally reliable.
questions.explanation: Multiple-choice options are written so that wrong answers sound plausible. Matching each option to the words in the lines is the reliable method.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 10 to 15. Why are people giving the couple unfriendly stares?
options: because Mr Ambrose is very tall and Mrs Ambrose wears a cloak
because the couple are famous
because the couple are walking in the road
questions.explanation: Lines 14 to 15 give the reason: the stare is aimed at “Mr. Ambrose’s height and upon Mrs. Ambrose’s cloak”. The June 2019 examiner report noted that unsupported inferences were unhelpful on Question 1; the multiple-choice format still rewards what the lines actually say.
questions.misconception: Choosing an answer that seems likely instead of one the lines support.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 15 to 21. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Mr Ambrose’s moving lips suggest he is deep in thought.
Mrs Ambrose’s fixed stare suggests sorrow.
Mrs Ambrose finds people brushing past her comforting.
Mrs Ambrose scorns the people she meets to stop herself crying.

questions.explanation: Lines 17 to 21 state each of the true points. The “friction of people brushing past her was evidently painful”, so the third statement is false.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 21 to 27. Why does Mrs Ambrose withdraw her arm once they have crossed?
options: She lets her tears come now that they are safely on the other side.
She is angry with her husband.
She has seen someone she knows.
questions.explanation: Lines 24 to 26 link the movement to her mouth beginning “to relax, to tremble” and the tears that follow. Nothing suggests anger or a meeting.
questions.misconception: Picking an option that fits the action but not the reason given in the text.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 27 to 30. Why does Mr Ambrose take a turn along the pavement?
options: He feels awkward standing beside a grief that is greater than his own.
He is bored and wants to see the river.
He is cross that she is crying in public.
questions.explanation: Lines 28 to 30 give the reason: “feeling it awkward to stand beside a grief that was greater than his”. The other options invent motives.

questions.prompt: Write your own Question 1-style item on lines 1 to 9: a question with 3 options, where only 1 option is supported by the text. Then explain why each wrong option is wrong.
questions.model: Model answer: Question: What would the writer advise you not to wear in these streets? Options: a long blue cloak / a pair of boots / a tall hat. Answer: a long blue cloak, because line 6 says it is better not “to wear a long blue cloak”. Boots are never mentioned. A tall hat is a trap: the text warns against being “very tall”, not wearing tall hats.
checklist: Asks about a detail found within lines 1 to 9
Gives exactly 1 option that the lines clearly support
Writes wrong options that are tempting but not supported
Explains each wrong option with reference to the text
questions.explanation: Writing distractors yourself shows you how they are built: they borrow words from nearby lines or change a single detail.

units.title: Question 2: how the writer uses language
units.summary: Question 2 gives you a short extract and asks how the writer uses language to describe something. Zoom in on precise words, explain their effects and link them to the focus.

questions.prompt: How many marks is Paper 1 Question 2 worth?
questions.explanation: Question 2 is worth 8 marks and tests AO2 for language.

questions.prompt: Which areas does the Question 2 bullet list suggest you could write about? Choose all that apply.
options: words and phrases
language features and techniques
sentence forms
the structure of the whole text
the writer’s life
questions.explanation: The bullets point you to individual word choices and techniques, and to sentence forms. Structure belongs to Question 3, and the writer’s life is never required.

questions.prompt: Focus: the heat of the march. Which quotation shows most clearly that the heat is oppressive?
options: “a suffocating heat”
“pale blue and very still”
“snow gleaming gently”
“the scraggy fruit trees”
questions.explanation: “suffocating” suggests heat so thick it stops the soldiers breathing. The other options describe the mountains or trees.

questions.prompt: Match each word or phrase to its effect.
pairs: the valley shines painfully bright in the heat
the heat seems to choke the soldiers
harsh light with nowhere to hide
the land looks flat and lifeless, like a drawing
questions.explanation: Each choice adds a different shade to the heat: brightness, breathlessness, harshness, lifelessness.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘The writer uses lots of adjectives like “white, hot road” to describe the heat. This makes the reader imagine it.’
Answer B: ‘The road is “white, hot”, as if bleached by the sun, and the rye “threw on a suffocating heat”: the verb “threw” makes the heat an attack aimed at the soldiers, and “suffocating” suggests it is choking them.’
options: Answer A, because it names a word class.
Answer B, because it explains what precise words suggest about the heat.
Answer A, because ‘imagine’ shows the effect on the reader.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A identifies and stops. Answer B zooms in on individual words and explains their effects, which is what the higher levels reward.

questions.prompt: The glossary says ‘knapsacks: soldiers’ backpacks’. A student writes: ‘The writer uses “knapsacks”, which means soldiers’ backpacks.’ Why is this weak?
options: It copies the glossary meaning instead of commenting on the effect of the writer’s words.
‘Knapsacks’ is not in the extract.
Glossary words must never be mentioned.
It is not weak: defining words earns marks.
questions.explanation: The June 2025 Paper 1 examiner report noted students copying a glossary definition as their comment. The glossary helps you understand; the marks come from explaining effects, such as knapsacks that “could burn no more”.
questions.misconception: Copying a glossary definition as the comment on effect.

questions.prompt: How do the mountains in lines 6 to 8 contrast with the valley?
options: They are cool and still, a calm, distant goal against the glittering heat of the valley.
They are hotter than the valley.
They are where the soldiers have come from.
They are covered in rye fields.
questions.explanation: The mountains are “pale blue and very still”, with snow “gleaming gently”. Their coolness makes the heat around the soldiers feel worse.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The knapsacks give off “a cold, prickly sensation”, so the weather has turned cold.’ What has the student misunderstood?
options: The knapsacks are so hot they can “burn no more”, so they feel cold and prickly: a sign of how overheated the soldiers are.
The quotation is about the mountains.
Nothing: the weather does turn cold.
‘Prickly’ refers to the rye.
questions.explanation: Words must be read in context. The June 2024 Paper 1 examiner report gave examples of single words lifted out of context and misread.

questions.prompt: Explain how the writer uses verbs in lines 1 to 15 to describe the heat.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The verbs make the heat active and hostile. The valley “glittered with heat”, a verb that suggests a hard, painful brightness rather than a pleasant shine. The rye “threw on a suffocating heat”, as though the crops are hurling it at the soldiers, and the knapsacks “could burn no more”, so the heat has reached a limit beyond pain. Together these verbs turn the landscape into an enemy pressing in on the marching men.
checklist: Picks out precise verbs such as “glittered”, “threw” or “burn”
Explains the connotations of each verb
Links the verbs to the focus on heat
Uses short, embedded quotations
questions.explanation: Verbs often carry the strongest effects in description. Explaining a few in depth beats listing many.

questions.prompt: Look in detail at lines 1 to 15. How does the writer use language here to describe the heat of the march? You could include the writer’s choice of words and phrases, language features and techniques, and sentence forms.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Lawrence makes the heat feel like an enemy that surrounds the soldiers. The road is “white, hot”, bleached of colour, and the trees offer only “a moment of shade, then out into the glare again”, so relief is brief and the harsh “glare” returns. The valley “glittered with heat”, and the fields spread in “a dull, hot diagram”: the metaphor of a diagram makes the countryside flat and lifeless, as though the heat has drained it. The rye “threw on a suffocating heat”, a verb of attack joined to an adjective of choking. The long final sentence builds physical detail upon detail, hot feet, sweat in the hair, until the knapsacks “could burn no more” and feel “cold, prickly”, a paradox that shows bodies pushed past normal sensation. Against all this the mountains are “very still” and gently snowy, so the heat seems even more cruel to men marching towards coolness they cannot reach.
checklist: Analyses the effects of individual word choices in detail
Selects precise, well-chosen quotations from lines 1 to 15
Uses terms such as metaphor, paradox or contrast accurately and as part of the explanation
Comments on a sentence form and what it does at that point
Keeps every point tied to the focus of the heat
questions.explanation: At the top level, every quotation is explained precisely and linked to the focus, and terms are used to sharpen the analysis rather than to decorate it.

units.title: Question 3: structure for one effect
units.summary: Since 2026, Question 3 names a single effect, such as tension. Track how the writer’s structural choices build or release that effect across the whole text.

questions.prompt: Since 2026, Paper 1 Question 3 asks you to write about structure and:
options: a single named effect, such as tension
the writer’s life
only the opening lines
language in a short extract
questions.explanation: AQA changed Question 3 so that it names one effect, for example asking how the structure creates tension or suspense.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each of these is a structural feature.

statements.s: a shift in focus
a pivotal point
a simile
a change in pace

questions.explanation: Shifts in focus, pivotal points and changes of pace are about the arrangement of the text. A simile is a language feature.

questions.prompt: Where is the pivotal point of the extract?
options: “But before he could cut the strings, it happened.” (line 27)
“He started to untie his moccasins.” (lines 21 to 22)
“The fire was a success.” (lines 6 to 7)
“He remembered the advice of the old-timer” (line 7)
questions.explanation: Line 27 divides the text into before and after: from here the disaster unfolds.

questions.prompt: Put these stages in the order the tension develops.
items: The man believes he is safe
Doubt creeps in as his fingers go lifeless
He struggles with the frozen strings
The snow falls and the fire is blotted out
questions.explanation: The tension rises from false security, through growing physical danger, to the disaster.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘At the beginning the man is safe, in the middle he unties his moccasins, and at the end the fire goes out.’
Answer B: ‘The repeated “He was safe” at the start builds false security, so when the narrative pauses to explain the spruce tree just before the snow falls, the delay stretches the tension until the fire is “blotted out”.’
options: Answer A, because it covers the whole text.
Answer B, because it explains how structural choices create tension.
Answer A, because it is in order.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A retells events. Answer B explains why things are placed where they are and how that builds tension.

questions.prompt: Which approach did the June 2022 Paper 1 examiner report criticise in structure answers?
options: Restricting comments to the beginning, middle and end, and recounting events
Tracking shifts in focus within the text
Explaining why an event is placed where it is
Linking a later moment back to an earlier one
questions.explanation: The June 2022 report noted answers limited to beginning, middle and end that missed the shifts inside the text. The other options describe what strong answers do.
questions.misconception: Retelling the text as beginning, middle and end instead of analysing structural choices.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention the old-timer’s advice in lines 7 to 11?
options: It plants a warning that the reader remembers when things go wrong, so the man’s confidence seems dangerous.
It introduces a new main character.
It ends the story.
It describes the weather.
questions.explanation: The man dismisses the warning, but the reader does not. Placing it early makes the later disaster feel like the warning coming true.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘In lines 28 to 35 the writer slows the pace, which makes it less tense.’ What is wrong?
options: Slowing down to explain the tree delays the disaster we sense is coming, which increases tension.
There is no change of pace in these lines.
These lines are about the dog.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: After “it happened”, the reader knows something has gone wrong but must wait to learn what. The delay heightens suspense.

questions.prompt: Explain how the writer uses a shift in focus from the man to the tree (lines 30 to 38) to create tension.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Just after “it happened”, the narrative turns away from the man to the spruce tree above him, and the pace slows to describe how each bough is “fully freighted” with snow. Moving the focus upwards makes the reader look where the man did not, and the step-by-step chain, one bough capsizing onto the next, builds like the avalanche it describes. The tension comes from watching a disaster we cannot stop, before the focus drops back down to the fire.
checklist: Identifies the shift in focus from the man to the tree
Explains how the shift and the slower pace build tension
Refers to precise points in the text
Uses structural terminology accurately
questions.explanation: Explaining a shift in focus means saying what we are made to look at, and why that matters at this point.

questions.prompt: How has the writer structured the text to create tension? You could write about how tension rises or falls by the end, how the writer uses structure to create an effect, and other structural features such as changes in mood or perspective.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): London structures the extract as a trap that closes slowly. It opens with false security: “He was safe” is repeated, and the fire is “a success”, so the reader relaxes with the man. The mood darkens through small reversals: “But it was surprising” introduces fingers going “lifeless”, and “All of which counted for little” pulls our attention back to the comforting fire, which makes the danger easier to forget. The pivotal sentence “it happened” comes before we know what “it” is, and the narrative then delays the answer, shifting focus upwards to the snow-laden spruce and explaining his mistake step by step. This slowing of pace builds suspense like the gathering avalanche, until the short, exclamatory “the fire was blotted out!” releases it. The final image of “fresh and disordered snow” leaves a blank where the fire was, so tension is higher at the end than at the start: the man’s survival is now in doubt.
checklist: Tracks how tension changes across the whole extract
Explains why key moments are placed where they are
Uses terms such as pivotal point, shift in focus and pace accurately
Refers to precise points in the text to support each claim
Keeps the focus on structure rather than language
questions.explanation: Top answers follow the named effect across the whole text and explain each structural choice that controls it.

units.title: Question 4: evaluating a statement
units.summary: Question 4 gives a statement about the text and asks how far you agree. Make a clear judgement, comment on the writer’s methods and support every point with references.

questions.prompt: How is Paper 1 Question 4 worded since 2026?
options: A statement is given directly, followed by ‘To what extent do you agree and/or disagree with this statement?’
‘A student said …’ followed by the statement
‘List 4 things …’
‘Compare the 2 sources …’
questions.explanation: AQA removed the reference to a student making the statement. The question now gives the statement directly.

questions.prompt: How many marks is Question 4 worth, and which assessment objective does it test?
options: 20 marks, AO4
8 marks, AO2
16 marks, AO3
40 marks, AO5 and AO6
questions.explanation: Question 4 is the biggest reading question on Paper 1: 20 marks for evaluation (AO4).

questions.prompt: Statement: ‘In this opening, Bertha’s happiness seems fragile rather than joyful.’ Which quotation best supports the view that her happiness is joyful?
options: “she wanted to run instead of walk”
“It was dusky in the dining-room and quite chilly”
“she could not bear the tight clasp of it”
“she’d forgotten it, as usual”
questions.explanation: Wanting to run and dance like a child shows energy and delight. The other quotations describe chill, discomfort or forgetfulness.

questions.prompt: Which quotations could support the view that her happiness is fragile or uneasy? Choose all that apply.
options: “it burned in your bosom”
“keep it shut up in a case like a rare, rare fiddle”
“It was dusky in the dining-room and quite chilly”
“to take dancing steps on and off the pavement”
“to bowl a hoop”
questions.explanation: Burning heat and a precious instrument shut in a case suggest something intense or delicate, and the cold, dim room hints at a threat. Dancing and hoops show uncomplicated joy.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘I agree that her happiness is fragile because Bertha is happy but then it is cold in the dining room.’
Answer B: ‘I partly agree. Bertha’s joy is real, she wants “to run instead of walk”, but Mansfield’s image of a body kept “in a case like a rare, rare fiddle” suggests something precious that must be protected, so her happiness already seems delicate.’
options: Answer A, because it agrees clearly.
Answer B, because it weighs the statement and explains how a method shapes the impression.
Answer A, because it mentions the setting.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer B makes a judgement, supports it with precise references and comments on the writer’s method. That is what evaluation means.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Question 4 matches what examiners have said?
options: You do not have to argue both sides; a focused, well-supported view can reach the top level.
You must disagree with at least half of the statement.
Background about the 1920s is required.
You should only write about the first 5 lines.
questions.explanation: The June 2019 and June 2025 Paper 1 examiner reports both said a counter-argument is not required, and the 2025 report warned against forcing disagreement without evidence.
questions.misconception: Believing you must always argue against the statement to show balance.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to the impression it creates.
pairs: “as though you’d suddenly swallowed a bright piece of that late afternoon sun”
her joy feels bright but also burning
frustration at having to behave properly
a comic detail that makes her seem scatty and childlike
“the cold air fell on her arms”
a chilly detail that hints at a threat to her warmth
questions.explanation: Evaluation depends on noticing how each method shapes your impression of the character.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Bertha is drunk, because the text says “drunk and disorderly”.’ What is wrong?
options: Bertha only wonders whether her joy can be shown without looking “drunk and disorderly”; she is not drunk.
The phrase is not in the extract.
Bertha admits she has been drinking.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: Reading a phrase out of its sentence leads to misreadings. The June 2022 Paper 1 examiner report gave the example of ‘hovering’ read as ‘hoovering’; careful reading of the whole sentence prevents this kind of error.

questions.prompt: Write the opening paragraph of an answer to this statement: ‘In this opening, Bertha’s happiness seems fragile rather than joyful.’ State your view and support it with at least 1 reference.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): I partly agree. At first Bertha’s happiness is joyful and childlike: she wants “to bowl a hoop” and laugh at nothing. However, Mansfield makes the feeling almost too strong to bear, describing it as if she has swallowed a piece of the sun that “burned” inside her, which suggests a happiness that is intense and perhaps dangerous rather than simply light.
checklist: States a clear view on the statement
Supports the view with at least 1 precise reference
Begins to comment on the writer’s method (such as imagery)
Sets up a line of argument that later paragraphs can develop
questions.explanation: A strong opening paragraph gives a clear judgement straight away and backs it up.

questions.prompt: ‘In this opening, the writer makes Bertha’s happiness seem fragile rather than joyful.’ To what extent do you agree and/or disagree with this statement? In your response, you could consider your own impressions of Bertha, comment on the methods the writer uses and support your response with references to the text. (In the exam this is worth 20 marks. Here, aim for 2 well-developed paragraphs.)
questions.model:
Model answer (Level 4): I largely agree, because Mansfield shows a joy so intense that it already seems at risk. At first the happiness is joyful: Bertha wants to dance on the pavement and “bowl a hoop”, childlike images of freedom. Yet the central metaphor is unsettling. She feels as if she has swallowed “a bright piece of that late afternoon sun”, and it “burned”, scattering sparks; the light is beautiful but also hot and uncontrollable. Her own image of a body kept “in a case like a rare, rare fiddle” adds to this: the repeated “rare” makes her feelings precious, but a fiddle in a case is shut away and easily damaged.

The setting and the structure strengthen the sense of fragility. Her joyful thoughts are interrupted by the practical exchange with Mary, “Yes, M’m”, as if ordinary life keeps cutting across her bliss. The paragraph then moves to a dining-room that is “dusky” and “quite chilly”, and “the cold air fell on her arms”: Mansfield places cold beside warmth, hinting that something could chill this happiness. So the opening is joyful on the surface, but the writer’s choices make that joy feel delicate, like something that may not survive.
checklist: Makes a clear, sustained judgement about the statement
Analyses how the writer’s methods shape impressions of Bertha
Uses precise, well-chosen references from across the extract
Explores more than one aspect, such as imagery, setting and interruptions
Develops an interpretation rather than listing points
questions.explanation: Top-level evaluation is confident and sustained, with methods and references woven into a clear argument.

units.title: Question 1: choosing true statements
units.summary: Paper 2 Question 1 asks you to choose 4 true statements from 8 about given lines of a source. The statements follow the order of the text, so check each one against the lines.

questions.prompt: In Paper 2 Question 1, how many statements should you choose?
options: 4 out of 8
2 out of 4
As many as you think are true
8 out of 8
questions.explanation: You choose a maximum of 4 statements from 8, and each correct choice earns 1 mark.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about Question 1 is true or false.

statements.s: The statements follow the order of the text.
Choosing more than 4 statements can cost you marks.
Papers from 2027 use tick boxes for this question.
You may use details from anywhere in the source.

questions.explanation: The June 2019 examiner report noted that the statements are in text order and that choosing more than 4 loses marks. AQA’s 2027 layout uses tick boxes. Only the lines named in the question count.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 1 to 9. Choose 4 statements below which are true.
options: The writer was not ready to set off until it was nearly October.
The writer expected warm weather on the high ground.
He wanted the means to camp out, even if he did not camp.
He found it relaxing to have to reach shelter by dusk.
He thought a village inn was always certain to welcome walkers.
He thought people travelling on foot could not always rely on an inn.
He thought a tent was troublesome to pitch.
He thought a tent was easy to hide among his baggage.
questions.explanation: Lines 1 to 9 support the 4 true statements. There was “no Indian summer to be looked for”, reaching shelter is “harassing”, an inn is “not always to be reckoned sure”, and a tent is “a conspicuous feature”. In the exam this question is worth 4 marks.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 9 to 19. Choose 4 statements below which are true.
options: A sleeping-sack is always ready to use.
The writer says a sleeping-sack serves only as a bed.
A sleeping-sack does not show passers-by that you plan to camp.
He thought keeping a camp secret was unimportant.
A camp that is not secret can attract visitors at bedtime.
In the end he decided on a tent.
The sack was made after several visits to Le Puy.
He was disappointed with the finished sack.
questions.explanation: It serves “a double purpose”, secrecy is “a huge point”, he “decided on a sleeping-sack”, and it was “triumphantly brought home”, so the other 4 statements are false.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Student A and Student B explain why they rejected the statement ‘He thought a tent was easy to hide among his baggage’.
Student A: ‘It sounded wrong.’
Student B: ‘Line 9 says a tent forms “a conspicuous feature in your baggage”. Conspicuous means easy to see, so the statement says the opposite.’
options: Student A, because instinct is usually right.
Student B, because the decision is checked against the exact words.
Student A, because it is quicker.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Statements are designed to look plausible. Testing each against the lines is the only reliable method.

questions.prompt: Line 16 says you must “sleep with one eye open”. Which statement is true?
options: You must stay alert and sleep lightly.
You should keep one eye physically open all night.
You will sleep very deeply.
questions.explanation: This is an idiom. The June 2025 Paper 2 examiner report noted students taking idioms literally, such as ‘in this neck of the woods’.
questions.misconception: Taking an idiom literally.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s attitude to the “convivial rustic” who “visits your bedside after an early supper”?
options: He finds such friendly visits a nuisance when he wants privacy.
He looks forward to meeting local people at night.
He is frightened of them.
He wants to hire them as guides.
questions.explanation: The visit is listed among the drawbacks of a camp that is “not secret”, a “troubled resting-place”. The humour is gentle, but the visits are unwelcome.

questions.prompt: A student chooses the statement ‘The sack was exactly 6 feet square.’ Why is this false?
options: The text says it was “nearly six feet square”.
The text says it was 6 feet long and 2 feet wide.
The size is never given.
questions.explanation: A single word such as ‘nearly’ can turn a true-looking statement false. Read every statement as carefully as the text.

questions.prompt: Read again lines 20 to 25. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The sack had flaps that served as a pillow at night.
The writer insists it was truly a sack.
It was made of green waterproof cloth on the outside.
It was lined with blue sheep’s fur.
He found it uncomfortable as a bed.

questions.explanation: It was “never a sack by more than courtesy”, so he does not insist it was a real sack, and it was “warm and dry for a bed”.

questions.prompt: Write 2 statements about lines 13 to 19, 1 true and 1 false but tempting. Explain how a careful reader would tell them apart.
questions.model: Model answer: True: ‘He travelled to Le Puy more than once while the sack was being made.’ False but tempting: ‘He believed a public camp gave a restful night.’ The false statement borrows the words “camp” and “resting-place” from line 14, but the text calls a public camp “a troubled resting-place”, so a reader who checks the exact phrase will reject it.
checklist: Writes 1 statement that the lines clearly support
Writes 1 false statement that reuses words from the text to tempt the reader
Explains which words in the text decide the matter
Keeps both statements within lines 13 to 19
questions.explanation: False statements often reuse the text’s own words with a small change. Writing them yourself trains you to spot the trick.

units.title: Question 2: inferring differences
units.summary: Question 2 asks what you can infer about the differences between 2 named things in Source A and Source B. Keep the named focus as the subject of your sentences and develop each inference.

questions.prompt: How many marks is Paper 2 Question 2 worth?
questions.explanation: Question 2 is worth 8 marks and tests AO1: interpreting both texts and bringing them together.

questions.prompt: Question: ‘The writers in Source A and Source B are describing different cabins on board ship. What can you infer about the differences between the 2 cabins?’ What must the answer focus on?
options: the differences between the 2 cabins
the writers’ feelings about travel
the language of Source A only
the history of steamships
questions.explanation: The focus is named in the question: the cabins. Every inference should be about them.

questions.prompt: Match each detail to a reasonable inference about the cabin.
pairs: “narrow bunks fold down from the walls”
the bed is awkward to reach
there is no natural view of the sea
questions.explanation: Each detail states something; the inference is what it lets you work out about the cabin.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: The cabin in Source A is clean and warm.
Dickens’s cabin had been booked in his name.
The cabin in Source A has a large window.
Dickens was astonished when he saw his cabin.

questions.explanation: Source A says “It is clean and warm” and “There is no porthole”. Dickens describes his “comical astonishment”, and a note names him and his wife.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘In Source A the writer is happy and in Source B Dickens is shocked. They both went on a boat.’
Answer B: ‘Source A’s cabin is cramped but carefully designed, with bunks that “fold down from the walls”, so every space has a purpose; Dickens’s bed, by contrast, is “a most inaccessible shelf”, suggesting a cabin where comfort has hardly been considered.’
options: Answer A, because it mentions both sources.
Answer B, because it makes developed inferences about the cabins from both texts.
Answer A, because it is shorter.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A is about the writers, not the cabins, and its difference is simple. Answer B keeps the cabins as the subject and develops each inference.

questions.prompt: A student writes mostly about how Dickens feels astonished and how the modern writer feels grateful. What is the problem?
options: The question is about the cabins; answers about the writers’ feelings rather than the named focus were held at Level 2.
Feelings are never relevant to Paper 2.
The student should only write about Source B.
There is no problem.
questions.explanation: The June 2022 and June 2023 Paper 2 examiner reports both noted answers about the writers’ experiences or feelings instead of the named focus, which were capped. The 2023 report advised making the focus the subject of each sentence.
questions.misconception: Writing about the writers’ feelings instead of the named focus.

questions.prompt: Which pair of details compares like with like?
options: Source A’s bunks “fold down from the walls”; Dickens’s bed is “spread like a surgical plaster on a most inaccessible shelf”.
Source A’s screen shows the bow; Dickens sailed in January.
Source A’s card key works first time; Dickens’s ship carried mail.
Source A cost £89; Dickens’s quilt was flat.
questions.explanation: Both details are about the beds, so the difference is meaningful. The June 2019 Paper 2 examiner report stressed comparing like with like.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Dickens’s cabin must have been grand because it was called a state-room.’ What is wrong?
options: Dickens puts “state-room” in inverted commas ironically: the very thin mattress and the inaccessible shelf show it is anything but grand.
The word does not appear in Source B.
Dickens says the cabin was grand.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: The grand name and the tiny reality clash. Reading the details around the word shows the irony.

questions.prompt: Write 1 developed paragraph inferring a difference between the beds in the 2 cabins.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): The beds suggest very different attitudes to the traveller’s comfort. In Source A the bunks are “made up with white sheets tucked as tight as envelopes”, which implies a cabin prepared neatly and in advance, ready for a tired passenger. Dickens’s bed, however, is “a very thin mattress” on “a most inaccessible shelf”, so it seems both uncomfortable and hard even to climb into. This suggests that the modern cabin is designed around the passenger, while the Victorian one leaves the passenger to cope.
checklist: Keeps the beds (the focus) as the subject
Uses a detail from each source
Moves from what the detail says to what it suggests
Develops the difference with a linking word such as ‘however’ or ‘whereas’
questions.explanation: The June 2025 Paper 2 examiner report described the move from paraphrase to inference to developed explanation; this paragraph does each of these.

questions.prompt: The writers in Source A and Source B are describing different cabins on board ship. What can you infer about the differences between the 2 cabins?
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The modern cabin is small but efficient and predictable, whereas Dickens’s state-room seems both tiny and badly thought out. In Source A everything is “bolted down or clipped in place”, suggesting a space designed for the movement of the sea, and the bunks “fold down from the walls” to save room. Even the lack of a window has been solved with a camera screen, so the designers have anticipated the passenger’s needs. Dickens’s cabin, by contrast, offers “a very thin mattress” spread “like a surgical plaster”, an image that makes the bed look clinical and stuck on rather than comfortable. The grand title of ‘state-room’ only stresses how little thought has gone into it. Finally, the modern writer finds the cabin “close to luxury” after a long day, which implies it meets modern expectations of clean comfort, while Dickens’s “astonishment” suggests his cabin falls far below what he had been led to expect.
checklist: Makes perceptive inferences about the cabins from both sources
Keeps the cabins as the focus throughout
Uses precise, well-chosen details from each source
Draws clear differences between like and like
Develops inferences instead of paraphrasing
questions.explanation: Top answers synthesise both texts around the named focus and develop each inference.

units.title: Question 3: language in non-fiction
units.summary: Question 3 asks how a non-fiction writer uses language to describe something, in given lines of 1 source. Explain why the writer chose these words, not just what they mean.

questions.prompt: How many marks is Paper 2 Question 3 worth?
questions.explanation: Question 3 is worth 12 marks for language analysis (AO2).

questions.prompt: What does Paper 2 Question 3 ask you to analyse?
options: language in given lines of 1 source
structure across both sources
the writers’ perspectives in both sources
your own writing
questions.explanation: It asks how the writer uses language to describe something in lines named in the question. Writing about other lines or the other source keeps the mark low.

questions.prompt: “Delight itself, however, is a weak term” (line 2). What does this suggest?
options: His feelings are so strong that ordinary words cannot express them.
He was disappointed by the forest.
He dislikes the word ‘delight’.
He was bored after a long day.
questions.explanation: By calling even ‘delight’ too weak, Darwin tells us his pleasure goes beyond normal language, which makes the forest seem extraordinary.

questions.prompt: Match each quotation to the method or effect it shows.
pairs: “A most paradoxical mixture of sound and silence”
contrast that makes the forest mysterious
“a little torrent flowed down the trunk”
a small image of great force
questions.explanation: Linking each quotation to a method and an effect is the core of language analysis.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘Darwin uses a list in lines 4 to 6 to show there are lots of things in the forest.’
Answer B: ‘The list “The elegance of the grasses, the novelty of the parasitical plants, the beauty of the flowers” piles up nouns of admiration, as if Darwin is trying one word after another, and it builds to “above all the general luxuriance”, which stresses the overwhelming richness of the forest.’
options: Answer A, because it names the feature.
Answer B, because it explains how the list works and what it builds to.
Answer A, because it is concise.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Answer A only says the list has many items. Answer B explains the kind of words chosen and the effect of the build-up.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘“admiration” shows Darwin admired the forest.’ Why is this comment weak?
options: It repeats the word in another form; it does not explain how the language creates the effect.
‘admiration’ is not in the given lines.
Darwin did not admire the forest.
It is not weak: it is accurate.
questions.explanation: The June 2023 Paper 2 examiner report gave examples of synonym-only comments such as ‘fearful force shows he was scared’. Ask why the writer chose this word and not another.
questions.misconception: Restating a word as a synonym instead of explaining its effect.

questions.prompt: Choose all the quotations that show the power of the tropical rain.
options: “a little torrent flowed down the trunk”
“never have been penetrated by common English rain”
“this violence of the rain”
“the shady parts of the wood”
“the beauty of the flowers”
questions.explanation: The torrent and the word “violence” stress force, and English rain is used as a mild comparison. Shade and flowers have nothing to do with the rain.

questions.prompt: A student says “common English rain” (line 16) shows Darwin thinks England is better than Brazil. What is the stronger reading?
options: ‘common’ means ordinary: English rain seems mild beside the tropical storm, which stresses how violent the Brazilian rain is.
Darwin is homesick for England.
‘common’ means shared by everyone in England.
The student’s reading is the strongest.
questions.explanation: The comparison is there to measure the storm. Reading the word in context avoids a claim the text does not support.

questions.prompt: Explain how the writer uses contrast in lines 7 to 11.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Darwin calls the forest “a most paradoxical mixture of sound and silence”, and the contrast makes it seem almost magical. The insects are so loud they can be heard from “a vessel anchored several hundred yards from the shore”, an exaggerated distance that stresses the noise, yet inside “a universal silence appears to reign”. The verb “reign” gives the silence power, as if it rules the inner forest. The contrast suggests a place too rich and strange to fit normal expectations.
checklist: Identifies the contrast between sound and silence
Explains the effect of specific words such as “paradoxical” or “reign”
Uses short, precise quotations
Links the contrast to the impression of the forest
questions.explanation: Contrast is a language method when you explain what the opposing words do to our picture of the subject.

questions.prompt: You now need to refer only to lines 1 to 21. How does the writer use language to describe the Brazilian forest? (In the exam this is worth 12 marks.)
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Darwin uses language to show a scientist overwhelmed by feeling. He begins by rejecting his own word, “Delight itself, however, is a weak term”, which suggests the experience goes beyond what ordinary language can hold. The list of abstract nouns, beginning with “elegance” and “novelty”, sounds like a naturalist cataloguing, yet each word is one of admiration, and the list builds to “above all the general luxuriance”, stressing abundance. The forest is presented as full of contradictions: “a most paradoxical mixture of sound and silence”, where insect noise carries to ships offshore while “a universal silence appears to reign” inside, the verb “reign” making the silence powerful. Even the storm becomes evidence of richness: the rain could never be matched by “common English rain”, and a “little torrent” runs down the trunk, a phrase that joins small and mighty. Darwin then explains the rain’s role in the “verdure” of the woods, so his language moves from wonder to scientific reasoning, presenting the forest as both thrilling and understandable.
checklist: Analyses the effects of precise word choices throughout the given lines
Uses terms such as list, contrast or paradox accurately and as part of the explanation
Selects short, judicious quotations from across lines 1 to 21
Explains how the language creates a particular impression of the forest
Shows awareness of the writer’s viewpoint as a naturalist
questions.explanation: Top answers explain a range of choices precisely and link them to an overall impression of the subject.

units.title: Question 4: comparing perspectives
units.summary: Question 4 asks you to compare the writers’ feelings and perspectives across both whole sources. Compare ideas first, then comment on the methods each writer uses to convey them.

questions.prompt: How many marks is Paper 2 Question 4 worth, and which assessment objective does it test?
options: 16 marks, AO3
12 marks, AO2
8 marks, AO1
20 marks, AO4
questions.explanation: Question 4 is worth 16 marks and tests AO3: comparing writers’ ideas and perspectives.

questions.prompt: Since 2026, what does the second bullet of Question 4 ask you to do?
options: comment on the methods the writers use to convey their feelings and perspectives
compare the methods of each writer line by line
summarise each source separately
evaluate a statement about one source
questions.explanation: AQA changed ‘compare’ to ‘comment on’ for methods. The comparison is of ideas and perspectives, supported by comments on methods.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about Source A is true or false.

statements.s: The writer says they did not work hard.
The writer names people who helped.
The writer believes effort alone explains success.
The writer ends with a metaphor.

questions.explanation: The writer says “I did work hard” but names Mrs Okafor and others who helped, and ends with the image of the climber and the rope. Effort matters, but it is not the whole answer.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best sums up Smiles’s perspective in Source B?
options: People improve mainly through their own efforts, and too much help can make them weaker.
Governments should do more to help people.
Success is mostly down to luck.
Charities are the true source of national strength.
questions.explanation: Smiles calls self-help “the root of all genuine growth” and says outside help “is often enfeebling”.

questions.prompt:
Which answer is stronger?
Answer A: ‘Source A is positive about help but Source B is negative about help.’
Answer B: ‘Both writers value effort, but they disagree about help: Smiles warns that “Help from without is often enfeebling”, a confident general claim, while the Source A writer names the particular people who helped, from a maths teacher to a cousin, to show that effort “needs somewhere to happen”.’
options: Answer A, because it gives a clear contrast.
Answer B, because it compares precise perspectives and comments on methods.
Answer A, because it covers both sources.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: ‘Positive’ and ‘negative’ are too blunt. Answer B finds the common ground and the disagreement, and shows how each writer conveys their view.

questions.prompt: A student compares the writers’ ideas well but never mentions how they express them. What have recent examiner reports said about this?
options: Answers without comment on methods tended to stay in the lower half of a level.
Methods are not needed for this question.
Methods only matter for Source B.
Such answers usually reach the top level.
questions.explanation: The June 2024 and June 2025 Paper 2 examiner reports both noted that missing methods kept marks in the lower half of a level.
questions.misconception: Comparing ideas without commenting on the writers’ methods.

questions.prompt: Match each method to an example from the sources.
pairs: a proverb used as an authority
“When my mum lost her job in Year 11”
“the inevitable tendency is to render them comparatively helpless”
questions.explanation: Naming the method precisely helps you explain how each writer persuades the reader of their perspective.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘Both writers think help from others is harmful.’ What is wrong?
options: Only Smiles sees outside help as weakening; Source A argues it is essential, ending with the image of someone holding the rope.
Neither writer mentions help.
Source A says help is harmful and Smiles disagrees.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: Misreading one source’s perspective breaks the whole comparison. Check each writer’s main claim before you compare.

questions.prompt: Write 1 paragraph comparing how the writers use their openings to set up their perspectives.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): Both writers open with a familiar idea about success, but they treat it differently. Smiles begins with the saying “HEAVEN helps those who help themselves” and calls it “a well-tried maxim”, presenting it as proven wisdom that the rest of his argument builds on. The Source A writer starts with a similar belief, that people want “a story about grit”, but only to question it: the short sentence “But it is not quite true” signals that the writer will challenge the very idea Smiles defends.
checklist: Compares the writers’ ideas, not just their topics
Comments on a method in each opening
Uses a reference from each source
Uses comparative linking words
questions.explanation: Comparing openings is a quick way to show the different starting points of 2 perspectives.

questions.prompt: For this question, you need to refer to the whole of Source A, together with the whole of Source B. Compare how the writers convey their different perspectives on success and help from others. (In the exam this is worth 16 marks.)
questions.model:
Model answer (Level 4): Both writers believe effort matters, but they disagree sharply about help. Smiles sees self-reliance as the root of all progress: he opens with the proverb “HEAVEN helps those who help themselves”, treating it as settled truth, and his confident general statements, such as “help from within invariably invigorates”, leave no room for doubt. He presents outside help as a danger, “enfeebling” people and making them “comparatively helpless”, so his perspective is moralising and certain.

The Source A writer is more personal and more sceptical of the grit story. Rather than abstract claims, the writer lists real supports, “Mrs Okafor”, a warm library, a bursary, a cousin, and the plain sentence “The difference is not character” rejects the idea, which Smiles holds, that success reveals moral worth. Where Smiles distrusts “institutions”, Source A shows a library and a bursary making effort possible. The closing metaphor, “remember who held the rope”, keeps praise for effort but insists on the people behind it. Smiles writes as a confident authority addressing the nation; the modern writer writes from experience, persuading through specific detail.
checklist: Compares the writers’ perspectives perceptively, including where they overlap
Analyses how each writer’s methods convey their perspective
Uses precise, well-chosen references from both sources
Keeps comparison running through the answer rather than writing about each source separately
Uses precise words to describe each perspective
questions.explanation: Top answers compare ideas throughout, explain methods and choose exact words for each perspective.

units.title: Writing: what earns the marks
units.summary: Question 5 on both papers is worth 40 marks: 24 for content and organisation (AO5) and 16 for technical accuracy (AO6). Stay on the task’s focus, shape your ideas and check your accuracy.

questions.prompt: How are the 40 marks for Question 5 split?
options: 24 for AO5 (content and organisation) and 16 for AO6 (technical accuracy)
20 for each
30 for AO5 and 10 for AO6
16 for AO5 and 24 for AO6
questions.explanation: On both papers, Question 5 gives 24 marks for AO5 and 16 for AO6.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: AO5 covers how well you organise your ideas.
AO6 covers spelling and punctuation.
AO6 covers the range of your vocabulary and sentence structures.
AO5 is only about handwriting.

questions.explanation: AO5 is about communication and organisation; AO6 is about vocabulary, sentences, spelling and punctuation. Handwriting is not an assessment objective, though it must be readable.

questions.prompt: According to the 2026 mark schemes, what happens to the AO5 mark if a response does not directly address the focus of the task?
options: It is capped at 12 marks, the top of Level 2.
It scores 0.
Only the AO6 mark is reduced.
Nothing changes.
questions.explanation: AQA’s 2026 mark schemes cap AO5 at 12 if the focus of the task is not directly addressed, so reading the task carefully protects a large share of the marks.

questions.prompt: Lines 4 to 7 of the student’s description contain a punctuation error. What is it?
options: A comma splice: “as if it had given up waiting, the departures board flickered” joins 2 sentences with only a comma.
An apostrophe is missing from ‘departures’.
‘orange’ is spelt wrongly.
Speech marks are missing.
questions.explanation: A full stop or semicolon is needed after ‘waiting’. Secure sentence demarcation is one of the first things AO6 looks for.

questions.prompt:
Which opening is stronger for a description of a bus station?
Opening A: ‘In this picture I can see a bus station. There is a clock and a pigeon. It is very early in the morning.’
Opening B: “The bus station was empty. Well, nearly empty.”
options: Opening A, because it describes the picture clearly.
Opening B, because its short correction draws the reader in and sets a quiet mood.
Opening A, because it gives more information.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Opening A lists what is in a picture. Opening B uses a crafted short sentence and a correction that hints at something to notice.

questions.prompt: Which opening sentence would examiners say damages the register of a description?
options: ‘In the image I can see a bus station with a clock.’
‘Dawn reached the bus station before the first bus did.’
‘The clock above the ticket office had stopped at 4.17.’
‘Nobody was waiting, but the doors opened anyway.’
questions.explanation: The June 2019 Paper 1 examiner report noted that phrases such as ‘In the image I can see …’ damaged the register of descriptions. Describe the place, not the picture.
questions.misconception: Describing the picture (‘In the image I can see …’) instead of the place.

questions.prompt: Which features of the student’s description would earn AO5 credit? Choose all that apply.
options: A short opening sentence followed by a correction: “Well, nearly empty.”
A sensory detail of smell: “diesel and cold coffee”
A single-line ending that leaves a sense of emptiness: “Nobody got off.”
The comma splice in lines 4 to 5
The use of the word ‘nice’ to describe the clock
questions.explanation: The first 3 options are deliberate choices that shape the description. The comma splice is an AO6 error, and ‘nice’ does not appear.

questions.prompt: A student says: ‘To get top marks for AO6, I should use as many semicolons and colons as possible.’ What is wrong with this?
options: AO6 rewards accurate punctuation used for effect; examiners have reported semicolons and colons used without control.
Semicolons are not allowed in Question 5.
AO6 does not include punctuation.
Nothing: more advanced punctuation always scores higher.
questions.explanation: The June 2019 Paper 1 report noted semicolons and colons used indiscriminately, and the June 2019 Paper 2 report found them more often wrong than right. Accuracy matters more than variety for its own sake.
questions.misconception: Believing that using lots of advanced punctuation automatically raises the AO6 mark.

questions.prompt: Rewrite lines 4 to 7 to correct the comma splice. Show 2 different correct ways.
questions.model: Model answer: 1. ‘Above the ticket office a clock had stopped at 4.17, its hands folded together as if it had given up waiting. The departures board flickered, orange letters appearing and disappearing, promising buses to places nobody was going.’ 2. ‘Above the ticket office a clock had stopped at 4.17, its hands folded together as if it had given up waiting; the departures board flickered, orange letters appearing and disappearing, promising buses to places nobody was going.’
checklist: Corrects the comma splice with a full stop and a capital letter
Shows a second correct method, such as a semicolon or a conjunction
Keeps the rest of the punctuation accurate
Keeps the meaning and the images of the original
questions.explanation: A full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction such as ‘while’ can all fix a comma splice. Choose the one that suits the rhythm you want.

questions.prompt: Continue the description after line 16 with 1 more paragraph of about 100 words that shifts the focus or the mood. Aim for Level 4.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The driver waited, engine shuddering, as if he too was unsure why he had come. Then the cleaner leaned her broom against a pillar and walked towards the open doors. She did not hurry. She climbed the steps and sat by the window, and for the first time the station was entirely still. The doors sighed again, more softly. As the bus pulled away, its lights slid across the puddles one last time, and the clock above the ticket office, still stuck at 4.17, kept watch over nobody at all.
checklist: Shifts the focus or the mood in a deliberate way
Uses precise, original imagery rather than clichés
Links back to details from earlier in the description
Varies sentence forms for effect
