Punctuates accurately throughout
questions.explanation: Higher-level description is shaped: it moves the reader’s attention on purpose, echoes earlier details and ends with control.

units.title: Planning in 5 minutes
units.summary: A quick plan decides your focus, audience and shape before you write. Spend about 5 minutes on it so you leave time to write and to check.

questions.prompt: AQA papers advise you to plan Question 5 before you start writing. How long is a sensible planning time within the 45 minutes?
options: about 5 minutes
about 20 minutes
no time at all
the whole of the reading time
questions.explanation: About 5 minutes is enough to settle your focus and shape and still leave time to write and check. This timing is a planning guide, not an AQA rule.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the plan in the text is true or false.

statements.s: The plan states a clear viewpoint.
The plan names the audience.
The plan includes a paragraph on the other side of the argument.
The plan is written in full paragraphs.

questions.explanation: Lines 3, 4 and 12 show the viewpoint, the audience and the other side. The plan uses brief notes, which is quicker than full sentences.

questions.prompt: Which line of the plan shows the writer thinking about register?
options: Lines 4 to 5: “so formal but lively”
Line 3: “The reward should be the learning”
Lines 8 to 9: “Once the payments stop, the effort stops”
Line 18: the reminder to proofread
questions.explanation: Register is the level of formality. The writer chooses a tone to suit adults and teenagers reading a news website.

questions.prompt: Put the plan’s sections in the order the article will follow.
items: Open with a scene of a student counting possible cash
Explain how money changes why people learn
Show that payments reward students who already have advantages
Deal with the other side of the argument
Suggest what would help instead
Return to the student from the opening
questions.explanation: The plan moves from a hook, through developed reasons and a counter-argument, to a solution and a cyclical ending.

questions.prompt:
Which plan is stronger for the task ‘Write a description of a market at dawn’?
Plan A: ‘Arrive at the market. Walk round. Buy breakfast. Go home.’
Plan B: ‘Focus on 1 stall-holder setting up. Zoom from the empty square to her hands unpacking crates. Mood moves from cold and grey to warm as the sun reaches the stall. End with the first customer.’
options: Plan A, because it covers the whole morning.
Plan B, because it gives the description a clear focus and a change of mood.
Plan A, because it is easier to follow.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Plan A is a recount of events. Plan B shapes a description, which is what the higher levels reward.

questions.prompt: A student spends 15 minutes writing a detailed plan in full sentences. What is the main risk?
options: There is less time to write and check; the June 2019 Paper 1 examiner report noted excessive planning.
Examiners will not read a plan.
Plans are marked separately and this one is too long.
There is no risk.
questions.explanation: A plan is a tool, not a draft. The June 2019 Paper 1 examiner report listed excessive planning among the problems seen in Question 5.
questions.misconception: Spending so long on a plan that the writing is rushed.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the plan to its purpose.
pairs: keeps the argument consistent from start to finish
shows awareness of objections before answering them
questions.explanation: Each line of a good plan does a job. If a line does nothing, cut it.

questions.prompt: A student plans a 9-paragraph article covering every argument they can think of. Why is this a problem?
options: Examiner reports warn that very long answers lose clarity and accuracy; a few developed ideas work better.
Articles must have exactly 5 paragraphs.
More arguments always score more.
It is not a problem.
questions.explanation: The June 2019 Paper 2 examiner report said writing at great length harmed clarity and accuracy, and the June 2024 report gave 3 or 4 sides as a guide.

questions.prompt: Write a 5-minute plan for this task: ‘Write the opening of a story about a lost key.’
questions.model: Model answer: Focus: a girl finds the key to her late grandad’s shed is missing on the day the house is sold. Perspective: first person, present tense. Opening: start in the moment, hand on the empty hook. Middle: search the kitchen drawer; a memory of grandad hanging the key there. Turning point: she notices fresh mud on her brother’s trainers. End the opening on a question, not a solution. Mood: quiet, then tense.
checklist: Chooses a narrow focus for an opening rather than a whole story
Decides perspective and tense
Plans a starting point in the middle of a moment
Includes a turning point or hook
Thinks about mood or atmosphere
questions.explanation: A story-opening plan needs a focus and a hook, not a full plot with an ending.

questions.prompt: Using the plan in the text, write the opening paragraph of the article (about 80 words).
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Maya has a calculator open and a grin on her face. A grade 7 in maths, she has worked out, would be worth £50 under her parents’ new scheme; a grade 9, £100. For the first time in her life she is excited about simultaneous equations. It sounds like a success story. But ask Maya in a year’s time, when the payments have stopped, whether she still loves algebra, and the grin may have gone. Paying teenagers for results buys effort for a while. It does not buy learning.
checklist: Opens with the scene planned in the text
Makes the viewpoint clear by the end of the paragraph
Uses a register suited to a news website
Varies sentence length for emphasis
Punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: A strong opening follows the plan, hooks the reader and sets up the viewpoint without stating every argument at once.

units.title: Paragraphs and cohesion
units.summary: Each paragraph should do one job, often signalled by a topic sentence. Linking words and echoes of earlier ideas make the whole piece flow.

questions.prompt: What is a topic sentence?
options: The sentence, usually first, that tells the reader what the paragraph is about
The last sentence of the whole piece
A sentence that asks a question
A sentence that contains a statistic
questions.explanation: A topic sentence signals the paragraph’s job, so the reader always knows where the argument is going.

questions.prompt: Match each linking word or phrase from the article to its job.
pairs: moves to something happening at the same time
questions.explanation: Discourse markers guide the reader through the argument. Choose them for their meaning, not just for variety.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the topic sentence of the paragraph in lines 10 to 13?
options: “However, the café is about more than saving money.”
“Every repaired kettle is one less thing in landfill.”
“they cheer when it goes up”
“Bring it to Mill Lane.”
questions.explanation: The first sentence announces the new idea, that the café is about more than money, and the rest of the paragraph develops it.

questions.prompt: Fill the gap with a suitable linking word: ‘Most repairs are quick. ___, some faults take several visits.’
questions.explanation: The second sentence contrasts with the first, so a linking word of contrast is needed.

questions.prompt:
Which paragraph opening links better to the article so far?
Opening A: ‘Also the café is good. Also people like it.’
Opening B: ‘The benefits do not stop at the door, however. Once people have learned to fix a lamp, many of them start mending things at home.’
options: Opening A, because ‘also’ adds a point.
Opening B, because it links back to the café and moves the argument forward.
Opening A, because it is short.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Repeating ‘also’ stacks points without connecting them. Opening B refers back to the café and extends the idea.

questions.prompt: A student adds subheadings such as ‘Reason 1’ and ‘Reason 2’ to an article. What did the June 2022 Paper 2 examiner report say about this?
options: Subheadings tended to break up the coherence of the argument; linked paragraphs work better.
Subheadings are required in every article.
Subheadings earn extra AO6 marks.
The report did not mention presentation.
questions.explanation: The June 2022 report noted that subheadings broke the coherence of arguments, and the June 2023 report noted weak linking between paragraphs.
questions.misconception: Using subheadings in place of linked paragraphs.

questions.prompt: Put these sentences in a cohesive order to form a paragraph.
items: Repair cafés also bring people together.
Strangers sit side by side at the tables.
Before long, they are swapping skills.
By the end of the morning, the room feels like a community.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence comes first, then each sentence builds on the one before, with time phrases showing the order.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The article has no real structure because it just ends with “Bring it to Mill Lane.”’ What have they missed?
options: The ending returns to the toaster and Mill Lane from the opening, a deliberate cyclical structure.
The article has no opening.
The ending introduces a new topic.
Nothing: the ending is random.
questions.explanation: The opening describes “toasters that no longer toast” in the hall “on Mill Lane”. Returning to them makes the article feel complete.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite these sentences as 1 linked paragraph, using a topic sentence and at least 2 linking words or phrases:
‘Repair cafés save money. They reduce waste. They teach skills. People make friends.’
questions.model: Model answer (Level 3): Repair cafés offer far more than cheap fixes. Most obviously, they save money, since a new belt costs much less than a new vacuum cleaner. They also reduce waste, because every mended item stays out of landfill. Just as importantly, they teach skills that people take home with them, and in the process strangers often become friends.
checklist: Begins with a topic sentence that sums up the paragraph
Uses at least 2 linking words or phrases
Combines the ideas into a flowing paragraph rather than a list
Punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: Linking words and a topic sentence turn separate statements into a developed paragraph.

questions.prompt: Write a new paragraph to go between lines 13 and 14 of the article. It should have a topic sentence and link to the paragraphs on either side.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Saving things from the tip is only part of the story, though. Many of the volunteers are retired, and the café gives them a place where their skills are suddenly in demand again. A former electrician who had not picked up a screwdriver in years now runs a queue of lamps every month, and he will tell anyone who asks that he looks forward to it all week. His table, like most of the others, is rarely quiet.
checklist: Opens with a topic sentence that links back to the previous paragraph
Develops a single idea with a specific example
Leads naturally into the next paragraph about what happens at the tables
Keeps the article’s tone and register
Uses accurate punctuation and varied sentences
questions.explanation: A paragraph that fits between 2 others must look backwards and forwards at once: that is cohesion.

units.title: Vocabulary: precise, not showy
units.summary: Choose the exact word for the job, even if it is simple. Examiners reward precise vocabulary and warn against long words used for show.

questions.prompt: Which word in line 19 shows most precisely how the curl sits on Meg’s cheek?
options: “stamped”
“dark”
“wet”
“each”
questions.explanation: ‘Stamped’ suggests the curl is pressed flat and fixed in place, like a mark made by a stamp. It is a simple word chosen exactly.

questions.prompt: What does ‘precise vocabulary’ mean in your own writing?
options: Choosing the exact word for the job, even if it is simple
Using the longest words you know
Using a word from a thesaurus in every sentence
Avoiding verbs
questions.explanation: Precision is about fit, not length. A short exact word beats a long vague one.

questions.prompt: Match each plainer phrase to the more precise word or phrase Mansfield uses.
questions.explanation: Each of Mansfield’s choices adds a shade of meaning. ‘Veiled’, for example, suggests something delicate and partly hidden.

questions.prompt: Which verb most precisely describes washing on a line in a strong wind making a sharp cracking sound?
options: snapped
moved
did
affected
questions.explanation: ‘Snapped’ captures both the movement and the sound. The other verbs are vague or wrong.

questions.prompt:
Which sentence is stronger?
Sentence A: ‘The resplendent, effulgent flowers burgeoned in a plethora of iridescent hues.’
Sentence B: ‘The roses had opened overnight, heavy enough to bend their stems.’
options: Sentence A, because the vocabulary is more ambitious.
Sentence B, because each word is exact and the image is clear.
Sentence A, because it has more adjectives.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Sentence A piles up showy words that blur the picture. Sentence B is plain but precise, and the reader can see it.

questions.prompt: Examiners have named some words as examples of contrived vocabulary used for show. Choose all the words below that appeared in those warnings.
options: plethora
lackadaisical
discombobulated
dawn
shimmer
questions.explanation: The June 2019 and June 2022 Paper 1 examiner reports both gave ‘plethora’ as an example, and the 2022 report added ‘lackadaisical’ and ‘discombobulated’. Ordinary words used precisely are safer and stronger.
questions.misconception: Believing that rare or long words automatically earn higher marks.

questions.prompt: Why is “Windless, warm, the sky without a cloud.” (lines 2 to 3) effective even though the words are simple?
options: The short, plain phrases make the perfect weather feel calm and certain.
It uses rare words.
It contains a simile.
It is the longest sentence in the extract.
questions.explanation: Simple words in short phrases can create a strong effect. Here they match the stillness of a perfect day.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The day was very, very, very nice.’ What is the main problem?
options: Repeating an intensifier adds no meaning; a precise word or detail would show what made the day good.
‘very’ should be spelt ‘vary’.
‘nice’ is a rare word.
There is no problem.
questions.explanation: Intensifiers such as ‘very’ tell the reader how strongly to feel without showing why. A precise detail does the job better.

questions.prompt: Rewrite this sentence with more precise vocabulary: ‘The nice old man walked slowly down the big street.’
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The old man shuffled along the high street, pausing at every bench as if each one were an old friend.
checklist: Replaces the vague adjectives ‘nice’ and ‘big’ with something exact or removes them
Chooses a more precise verb than ‘walked slowly’
Adds a detail that shows character
Avoids showy or contrived words
questions.explanation: A precise verb such as ‘shuffled’ can replace a verb and an adverb together.

questions.prompt: Write about 80 words describing a place getting ready for an event, using precise vocabulary. Aim for Level 4.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): By 9am the village hall smelled of floor polish and urns of tea. Trestle tables stood in rows under paper bunting that sagged between the beams. Mrs Achebe tugged a tablecloth straight, then tugged it again. In the kitchen someone was slicing lemons, and the knife knocked steadily against the board. Outside, a van reversed up to the door, beeping, its back doors already open on a stack of folding chairs.
checklist: Chooses exact nouns and verbs rather than general ones
Uses sensory detail that is specific to the place
Avoids contrived or showy vocabulary
Varies sentence length
Spells and punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: At Level 4, vocabulary is extensive and well chosen: each word earns its place.

units.title: Sentence forms for effect
units.summary: Vary sentence forms on purpose: a short sentence can mark a turning point, a long one can build momentum. Control matters more than variety for its own sake.

questions.prompt: “He was safe.” (line 7) is:
options: a simple sentence
a compound sentence
a complex sentence
a minor sentence
questions.explanation: It has one main clause, so it is a simple sentence.

questions.prompt: Match each sentence type to an example from the text.
pairs: “No wind had blown for weeks, and each bough was fully freighted.”
“When he touched a twig, he had to look and see whether or not he had hold of it.”
questions.explanation: Recognising sentence types in published writing helps you use them with purpose in your own.

questions.prompt: Why might the writer repeat “He was safe.” (lines 1 and 7)?
options: To show the man reassuring himself, which makes the reader start to doubt it
To fill space
To show the fire has gone out
To introduce a new character
questions.explanation: Repetition of a short, confident sentence can sound like self-persuasion, which builds unease in the reader.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: A minor sentence has no main verb.
A complex sentence contains a subordinate clause.
Short sentences always create tension.
Varying sentence length can control pace.

questions.explanation: Sentence forms have no fixed effect; it depends on where and how they are used.

questions.prompt:
Which version of a tense moment is stronger?
Version A: ‘The door opened. A man came in. He sat down. He looked around. He ordered tea.’
Version B: ‘The door opened. For a long moment nobody moved, while the rain blew in across the tiles and the man in the doorway looked from face to face. Then he smiled.’
options: Version A, because short sentences build tension.
Version B, because it varies sentence length to slow the moment and then release it.
Version A, because it is clearer.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Version A repeats the same pattern until it becomes flat. Version B uses a long sentence to stretch time and a short one to land the surprise.

questions.prompt: A student starts every paragraph with 3 one-word sentences, such as ‘Cold. Dark. Silent.’ What did examiners report about this kind of habit?
options: Formulaic patterns of short fragments, repeated through a piece, became predictable and lost effect.
It always earns Level 4 for AO6.
It is required in descriptive writing.
Examiners have never commented on it.
questions.explanation: The June 2024 Paper 1 examiner report described formulaic triples such as ‘Scorching. Melting. Painful.’ being repeated, and the June 2025 report noted fragments that lost meaning.
questions.misconception: Repeating a fixed pattern of minor sentences in place of genuine variety.

questions.prompt: In lines 35 to 40, each sentence picks up from the one before (“This fell on the boughs beneath”, “This process continued”), and the passage ends with a long sentence joined by ‘and’. What is the effect?
options: The linked sentences mirror the snow falling from bough to bough, building to the disaster.
It makes the moment calm and peaceful.
It shows the man is asleep.
It has no effect.
questions.explanation: Each sentence starts where the last one ended, as one bough tips onto the next, and the final long sentence gathers speed like the avalanche it describes.

questions.prompt: A student writes ‘Because the fire went out.’ as a sentence in a story. What is wrong?
options: It is a fragment: a subordinate clause with no main clause, so it does not make sense alone.
‘Because’ is spelt wrongly.
It needs an exclamation mark.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: A minor sentence can be deliberate, but a subordinate clause on its own usually reads as an error.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite these sentences as 1 complex sentence followed by 1 short sentence for effect:
‘The man lit the fire. He felt proud. Snow fell from the tree. The fire went out.’
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): As the flames took hold, the man sat back and allowed himself a moment of pride, never thinking to look at the heavy branches above him. Then the snow fell.
checklist: Writes a correctly punctuated complex sentence
Follows it with a short sentence that lands the turning point
Keeps the meaning of the original
Uses the contrast in length deliberately
questions.explanation: A long build-up followed by a short sentence is a controlled way to create a turning point.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph of about 80 words describing a sudden change, using at least 3 different sentence forms for effect.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): All afternoon the beach had been loud with radios and shrieking children. Then the wind turned. It came off the sea in a long grey push, flattening the windbreaks and sending a red umbrella cartwheeling towards the dunes. Parents shouted names. Within minutes the sand was bare. Only the umbrella remained, lodged upside down against a fence, spinning slowly. Silence, almost.
checklist: Uses at least 3 sentence forms (for example compound, complex, simple, minor)
Places a short sentence at the turning point
Uses a long sentence to build movement or detail
Punctuates every sentence accurately
Makes each choice serve the change being described
questions.explanation: At Level 4, sentence forms are varied and controlled, and each one serves the effect at that point.

units.title: Paper 1 Q5: description from your imagination
units.summary: The description task asks you to describe a place or scene from your imagination; the picture is optional. Shape the description with a clear focus and a controlled mood.

questions.prompt: Since 2026, how is the description option in Paper 1 Question 5 worded?
options: Write a description from your imagination; you may choose to use the picture for ideas.
Describe exactly what is in the picture.
Write a description of a real place you have visited.
Write a description in the form of a letter.
questions.explanation: The 2026 change makes clear that the picture is only a starting point. The description must still address the focus of the task.

questions.prompt: Which assessment objective rewards the shape and organisation of your description?
options: AO5
AO6
AO2
AO4
questions.explanation: AO5 (24 marks) covers communication and organisation; AO6 (16 marks) covers technical accuracy.

questions.prompt: How does Woolf structure her description in lines 1 to 28?
options: She zooms in on the flower-bed and the light moving across tiny details, then pulls out to the people walking past.
She walks round the gardens from left to right.
She describes a whole day from morning to night.
She tells the history of Kew Gardens.
questions.explanation: The focus starts close, follows the light and then lifts “into the eyes of the men and women”, changing scale.

questions.prompt: Choose all the details that show Woolf looking very closely at small things.
options: “the shell of a snail with its brown, circular veins”
“the branching thread of fibre beneath the surface”
“staining an inch of the brown earth”
“the men and women who walk in Kew Gardens in July”
“a curiously irregular movement”
questions.explanation: Each correct option zooms in on something tiny, seen up close. The people are seen from a wider view.

questions.prompt:
Which opening is stronger for a description of a park in summer?
Opening A: ‘The park was nice. There were trees and people. The sun was shining and everyone was happy.’
Opening B: ‘Light dropped through the plane trees in coins and shook whenever the wind moved.’
options: Opening A, because it sets the scene clearly.
Opening B, because its precise, original image makes the reader see the light.
Opening A, because it mentions people.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Opening A is general and tells us how to feel. Opening B creates a specific picture with an original image.

questions.prompt: A student describes the picture from left to right: ‘On the left there is a tree. In the middle there is a bench. On the right there is a bin.’ What did the June 2023 Paper 1 examiner report say about this kind of answer?
options: Tour-like descriptions that walk round the picture lack a shaping structure.
It is the best way to organise a description.
Examiners prefer descriptions that follow the picture exactly.
The report did not comment on structure.
questions.explanation: The June 2023 report described tour-like descriptions walking round the picture, and the June 2022 report noted lists of picture details without structural links.
questions.misconception: Describing the picture item by item instead of shaping the description.

questions.prompt: Match each of Woolf’s methods to its effect.
pairs: the colours flicker and return like the moving light
the light “settled upon the flesh of a leaf”
the light seems alive and exploring
“one expected them to burst and disappear”
a moment of tension inside a single raindrop
the scale changes from tiny to human
questions.explanation: Woolf’s methods are worth borrowing: a moving focus and tension in tiny things.

questions.prompt: A student plans a beach description: arrival, swimming, lunch, a storm, a rescue, an ambulance, home. What is the problem?
options: It is a recount crammed with events; a description should focus on a moment or place and shape it.
It has too few events.
Beaches are not allowed as a topic.
There is no problem.
questions.explanation: The June 2022 report warned against cramming many events into one piece, and the June 2023 report noted recount structures in descriptions.

questions.prompt: Write the first 3 sentences of a description of a garden at night, using a zoom-in structure like Woolf’s.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Above the garden the sky was a deep, clean blue, scratched with the first stars. Below it the lawn had lost its colour, and the apple tree stood as a dark shape with one pale fruit still hanging. On that fruit a single snail was making its slow, silver way towards the stalk.
checklist: Starts with a wide view
Narrows the focus step by step
Ends on a small, precise detail
Uses original imagery
Punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: Zooming in gives a description a clear shape and leads the reader to a detail that matters.

questions.prompt: Write a description of a busy railway station from your imagination. In the exam this task is worth 40 marks; here, write about 150 words.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The departures board clicks over, and 200 heads tilt up at once. Platform 4. The crowd moves like water finding a gap, suitcases rumbling behind it. A woman in a green coat walks against the flow, holding a paper cup high above the shoulders that bump past her. Near the barriers a busker plays the same 4 bars again and again, and his open case holds 3 coins and a bus ticket. Then the focus narrows: a small boy sits on a rucksack beside a pillar, counting the trains on his fingers, untouched by the hurry around him. The tannoy crackles an apology. Somewhere a whistle blows. The boy’s father kneels beside him, and together they watch the long silver train slide in, its windows sliding past like the pages of a book being turned.
checklist: Creates original, precise imagery rather than clichés
Shapes the description deliberately, for example by narrowing the focus
Controls the mood and the pace
Uses a range of sentence forms for effect
Spells and punctuates accurately, including ambitious words
questions.explanation: Level 4 descriptions are compelling and crafted: the structure guides the reader, and every image is chosen with care.

units.title: Paper 1 Q5: writing a story opening
units.summary: The narrative option may ask for the opening of a story. Establish a voice and a situation, start close to a moment of interest and leave the reader wanting more.

questions.prompt: Since 2026, what may the narrative option in Paper 1 Question 5 ask you to write?
options: the opening of a story about a given topic
a complete novel
a diary entry about your own day
a newspaper report
questions.explanation: The 2026 sample paper asks for the opening of a story. You do not need to reach an ending.

questions.prompt: What narrative perspective does Buchan use?
options: first person
second person
third person
a mixture of all of these
questions.explanation: The narrator says “I returned from the City”, so it is a first-person narrative.

questions.prompt: What does the first sentence (lines 1 to 2) establish?
options: a narrator and his bored, disgusted mood
the solution to a mystery
a description of the weather in Africa
a conversation between friends
questions.explanation: We meet the narrator at a precise time, “pretty well disgusted with life”, which sets up his restlessness.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: Hannay is 37 years old.
Hannay grew up in England.
He has enough money to have a good time.
He has many close friends in London.

questions.explanation: He was taken from Scotland at 6 and has never been home since; he has “no real pal to go about with”.

questions.prompt:
Which story opening is stronger for ‘The lost key’?
Opening A: ‘I woke up at 7 o’clock. I got dressed and had breakfast. Then I went to school.’
Opening B: ‘The key was not on its hook. Mum’s keys were there, and the spare for Gran’s, but the small brass one had gone, and only I knew what it opened.’
options: Opening A, because it is in time order.
Opening B, because it starts in the moment and creates a mystery.
Opening A, because it is realistic.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Opening A is a recount of a routine. Opening B begins at a moment of interest and plants a question in the reader’s mind.

questions.prompt: Which choice did the June 2025 Paper 1 examiner report say tended to score better in narratives?
options: focusing on an episode or moment in time rather than a whole life story
ending with ‘it was all a dream’
using long stretches of dialogue
including as many events as possible
questions.explanation: The 2025 report found that episodes and moments in time scored better, and warned against rushed whole narratives and ‘it was a dream’ endings. The June 2024 report noted too much direct speech.
questions.misconception: Trying to fit a whole story, with lots of events and dialogue, into one answer.

questions.prompt: Match each of Buchan’s methods to its effect.
pairs: “as flat as soda-water that has been standing in the sun”
a simile that makes London seem dull and lifeless
talking to himself shows his frustration
“But from the first I was disappointed with it.”
a turning point after his high hopes
“the best bored man in the United Kingdom”
a humorous exaggeration that ends the paragraph
questions.explanation: A strong opening builds voice and situation through precise choices like these.

questions.prompt: A student says the opening has no hook because nothing exciting happens. What have they missed?
options: A narrator restless enough to want to “clear out” makes the reader expect something to break the boredom; the restlessness itself is the hook.
There is a murder in the first line.
The opening ends with a cliffhanger about a bomb.
Nothing: there is no hook.
questions.explanation: Openings can hook through character as well as action. A bored adventurer is a promise that adventure is coming.

questions.prompt: Write the first 3 sentences of a story opening that begins in the middle of a moment.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): The lift stopped between the fourth and fifth floors with a soft clunk, and the lights flickered once. Nobody spoke. Beside me, the man with the parcel tightened his grip on it until the brown paper creased.
checklist: Begins in the middle of an action or moment
Establishes a setting quickly
Creates a question or tension for the reader
Uses precise detail
Punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: Starting in the moment saves time and gives the opening immediate energy.

questions.prompt: Write the opening of a story about someone who is bored with their life. In the exam this task is worth 40 marks; here, write about 150 words.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Every Tuesday, Kiran Desai counted the ceiling tiles in Meeting Room B. There were 48, one of them cracked in the shape of Italy, and by the time Mr Pratt reached item 6 on the agenda, Kiran had usually toured the whole country. Today Italy had a new stain. He found himself oddly moved by it. After 12 years at Harlow & Webb, Kiran had learned to recognise the small changes: a new brand of biscuit, a stapler moved 2 desks along. Nothing large ever changed. That was the point of the place. So when the fire alarm went off at 10.14 and everyone filed obediently into the car park, Kiran did not stop with the others by the bins. He kept walking past the barrier and the bus stop, and turned left onto a road he had driven past every morning for 12 years without once wondering where it went.
checklist: Creates a distinctive narrative voice
Establishes a character and situation through precise detail
Controls pace, moving from routine to a turning point
Ends the opening with momentum rather than a full resolution
Spells and punctuates accurately, with varied sentences
questions.explanation: Level 4 openings have a convincing voice, a crafted structure and an ending that leaves the reader wanting more.

units.title: Paper 2 Q5: writing to argue a viewpoint
units.summary: Paper 2 Question 5 asks you to argue your viewpoint on a statement, in a set form for a named audience. Build one clear, developed argument and answer objections within it.

questions.prompt: What does Paper 2 Question 5 ask you to do?
options: Present your viewpoint on a statement in a specified form for a specified audience
Describe a picture
Compare 2 sources
Write the opening of a story
questions.explanation: The task gives a statement, a form (such as an article or speech) and an audience. You argue your own point of view.

questions.prompt: Which assessment objective rewards matching your tone and register to the audience?
options: AO5
AO6
AO3
AO1
questions.explanation: AO5 covers communication, including tone, style and register for the form, purpose and audience.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s viewpoint in the article?
options: Lunch should go back to 1 hour, even if the day finishes later.
Lunch should be cut further.
The canteen food is poor.
Students should go home at lunchtime.
questions.explanation: Lines 18 to 19 make the proposal explicit: “return lunch to 1 hour, and finish the day 25 minutes later”.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to an example from the article.
pairs: “Some will say a longer lunch simply means more time for trouble.”
questions.explanation: Each technique does a job in the argument. Naming them helps you plan your own.

questions.prompt:
Which opening is stronger for the same task?
Opening A: ‘Picture this. It is an incontrovertible truth that lunch is important. In this article I will be telling you why.’
Opening B: “At 12.40 the bell goes. By 12.45 the queue for the canteen stretches past the library.”
options: Opening A, because it uses impressive vocabulary.
Opening B, because a concrete scene draws the reader straight into the problem.
Opening A, because it tells the reader what to expect.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: The June 2023 Paper 2 examiner report named openers such as ‘Picture this …’ and ‘It is an incontrovertible truth that …’ as formulaic. Opening B shows the problem instead of announcing it.

questions.prompt: A student adds ‘97% of students say longer lunches improve grades’ to their article. What did the June 2025 Paper 2 examiner report say about this kind of detail?
options: Spurious invented statistics undermined responses; specific, believable examples work better.
Statistics always earn extra marks.
Every article must contain at least 1 statistic.
The report did not mention statistics.
questions.explanation: The 2025 report listed spurious invented statistics among the weaknesses in Question 5. A believable detail, like the queue past the library, persuades better.
questions.misconception: Inventing statistics to sound authoritative.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of the article in order.
items: A scene that shows the problem
A concession to the other side
What has been lost
A counter-argument answered
A proposal and conclusion
questions.explanation: The article builds its case step by step and saves the proposal for the end, where it has most force.

questions.prompt: A student argues for longer lunches in 1 paragraph, against them in the next, and for them again in the third. What is the problem with this approach?
options: Flip-flopping between sides weakens an argument; keep 1 clear viewpoint and deal with objections within it.
It shows balance and earns top marks.
Every paragraph must change sides.
Examiners have not commented on it.
questions.explanation: The June 2022 Paper 2 examiner report noted flip-flopping between sides. Answering an objection is different from switching sides.

questions.prompt: Write a paragraph that raises and answers a counter-argument to this statement: ‘Schools should ban mobile phones completely.’
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Some parents will say that their child needs a phone for safety, especially on the walk home. That worry is understandable. But a ban during the school day does not take phones away from journeys: students can hand them in at the gate in the morning and collect them at 3.15. The safety argument is about the street, not the classroom, and it is in the classroom that phones do most damage to concentration.
checklist: Raises a fair counter-argument
Acknowledges it before answering
Answers it with a clear, reasoned point
Returns to the writer’s own viewpoint
Uses accurate punctuation and varied sentences
questions.explanation: Dealing with an objection fairly and then answering it makes an argument more convincing.

questions.prompt: ‘Homework does more harm than good.’ Write an article for a school website in which you argue your point of view on this statement. In the exam this task is worth 40 marks; here, write about 180 words.
questions.model:
Model answer (Level 4): It is 9.40pm and Leon is still at the kitchen table, staring at a worksheet he does not understand. He has football training at 7am. His teacher, meanwhile, will spend part of tomorrow morning marking answers Leon guessed. Nobody in this picture is learning much.

I am not arguing that all homework should go. Reading a novel, or practising for a test you know is coming, can be valuable. But too much of what we are set is busywork: tasks that fill a box on a planner rather than a gap in our understanding. Busywork does harm, because it takes time from sleep and from the things that make us want to learn in the first place.

Some will say that homework builds discipline. Perhaps it does, when it is purposeful. Discipline is not built by copying a diagram at 10pm.

So here is a modest proposal: less homework, better homework. Ask us to read and to think. Then let Leon go to bed.
checklist: Presents a clear, convincing viewpoint from the start
Develops ideas with specific, believable examples
Organises paragraphs fluently, with a counter-argument answered
Uses a register and tone that suit a school website
Varies sentence forms and punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: Level 4 argument writing is convincing and crafted: a clear viewpoint, developed ideas, fluent paragraphs and a tone that suits the audience.

units.title: Forms for Paper 2 Q5 (1): article and letter
units.summary: Use the conventions that matter for the form: a headline or opening that hooks for an article, a greeting and sign-off for a letter. Do not waste time on columns, pictures or addresses.

questions.prompt: Which features show that this text is a letter?
options: a greeting (‘Dear Editor,’) and a formal sign-off (‘Yours faithfully,’)
a headline and columns
stage directions
a list of sources
questions.explanation: A greeting and a sign-off are the essential conventions of a letter.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

statements.s: An article can open with a headline.
A letter to a newspaper should be signed off.
You should draw columns and pictures for an article.
Full postal addresses earn most of the marks in a letter.

questions.explanation: Examiners reward the writing, not the layout. The June 2022 Paper 2 examiner report noted columns and pictures wasting time.

questions.prompt: What is the job of lines 2 to 3?
options: They state clearly what the letter is responding to.
They describe the writer’s grandmother.
They give a statistic.
They end the letter.
questions.explanation: A clear first line tells the editor and readers at once why the letter has been written.

questions.prompt: Which methods does Priya use to persuade? Choose all that apply.
options: inviting councillors to see for themselves
a personal example (her grandmother)
conceding a point before answering it
invented statistics
insults aimed at the council
questions.explanation: She invites councillors to ride the bus, mentions her grandmother and admits “the council has hard choices to make”. She uses no statistics or insults.

questions.prompt:
Which letter opening is stronger?
Opening A: ‘Hi, I’m Priya and I think the bus thing is rubbish lol.’
Opening B: “I am writing about last week’s report that the number 42 bus will stop running after 7pm from September.”
options: Opening A, because it is friendly.
Opening B, because its register suits a letter to a newspaper and it states the issue clearly.
Opening A, because it is shorter.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Opening A uses a register far too casual for the audience. Opening B is clear and formal.

questions.prompt: The task asks for a letter to a newspaper. A student writes a speech beginning ‘Ladies and gentlemen’. What is the main problem?
options: It ignores the form and audience set by the task, which affects the AO5 mark.
Speeches are never allowed in Paper 2.
It should begin ‘Hi everyone’.
There is no problem.
questions.explanation: The June 2024 Paper 2 examiner report noted responses that ignored the named audience. Read the form and audience as carefully as the statement.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the form and audience named in the task.

questions.prompt: Why does Priya mention “nurses finishing a shift at the hospital” and her grandmother?
options: Specific, human examples make the cost of the cut real to readers.
To show she knows a lot of nurses.
To change the subject.
To make the letter longer.
questions.explanation: Concrete examples persuade better than general claims. Readers can picture these people losing their way home.

questions.prompt: A student says Priya’s letter is weak because she admits “the council has hard choices to make”. What have they missed?
options: Conceding a fair point makes her seem reasonable, and she immediately turns it with ‘However’.
The phrase is not in the letter.
She agrees with the council completely.
Nothing: the admission ruins the argument.
questions.explanation: A concession followed by a rebuttal is a classic persuasive structure. It shows the writer has thought about the other side.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the opening of Priya’s letter as the opening of a newspaper article, with a headline.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): Headline: The last bus home. Every Thursday at 9pm, my grandmother waits at the stop outside the church hall with her choir music in a carrier bag. From September, she will be waiting for nothing. The council plans to stop the number 42 after 7pm, calling the evening service ‘underused’. Anyone who has ridden it knows that is not the whole story.
checklist: Writes a headline that suits the content
Opens with a hook such as a scene or a person
States the issue clearly within the first few sentences
Shifts from letter conventions to article conventions
questions.explanation: Changing the form changes the opening: an article hooks readers rather than addressing an editor.

questions.prompt: Write a letter to your local newspaper arguing for or against this statement: ‘Town centres should be closed to cars.’ In the exam this task is worth 40 marks; here, write about 180 words.
questions.model:
Model answer (Level 4): Dear Editor,

Your article last week asked whether our town centre should be closed to cars. As someone who walks through it every day, I believe it should, at least on weekends.

On a Saturday, the High Street is a queue of engines. Shoppers squeeze between bumpers, and the café on the corner has given up putting tables outside because nobody wants to eat beside an exhaust pipe. The street could be somewhere people want to spend time; instead it is somewhere they want to get through.

I accept that some shop owners fear losing customers who drive. Their concern deserves an answer, and there is one: the car park behind the library is rarely full, and a frequent shuttle bus would bring drivers within a 2-minute walk of every shop.

A car-free centre would not empty our town. It would give it back to the people who use it. I urge the council to try it for a summer and see.

Yours faithfully,

Amir Haddad
checklist: Uses letter conventions without wasting time on addresses
States a clear viewpoint early
Develops the argument with specific, believable detail
Answers a counter-argument
Uses a formal register and accurate punctuation
questions.explanation: Level 4 letters match their register to the audience and build a clear, developed argument.

units.title: Forms for Paper 2 Q5 (2): speech and essay
units.summary: A speech is written to be heard: address your listeners and guide them with signposts. A formal essay is more impersonal and builds its case in careful paragraphs.

questions.prompt: Which feature shows most clearly that this text is a speech?
options: It addresses the listeners directly: “Good evening, councillors.”
It has a headline.
It is signed ‘Yours sincerely’.
It has subheadings.
questions.explanation: Direct address to an audience who are present is the clearest sign of a speech.

questions.prompt: Match each speech feature to an example.
pairs: “Where are young people supposed to go?”
questions.explanation: Speeches use features like these because listeners cannot reread; the writer must guide them as they hear.

questions.prompt: How should a formal essay differ from a speech on the same topic?
options: It uses a more impersonal tone, with fewer direct appeals to listeners.
It uses more slang.
It must be written in the second person throughout.
It has no paragraphs.
questions.explanation: An essay builds its argument in measured paragraphs and usually avoids addressing the reader as a crowd.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each statement about the speech is true or false.

statements.s: Daniel introduces himself to build trust.
He refuses to accept that there are any objections.
He ends by thanking his audience.
He uses statistics to support his case.

questions.explanation: Daniel says “Those are fair concerns” and uses no statistics; he relies on everyday examples and fairness.

questions.prompt:
Which speech ending is stronger?
Ending A: ‘That is the end of my speech. Thanks.’
Ending B: “We are not asking you to solve every problem young people face. We are asking for one place that is ours.”
options: Ending A, because it is clear that the speech has finished.
Ending B, because the repeated structure narrows the request to something modest and memorable.
Ending A, because it is polite.
Both are equally strong.
questions.explanation: Ending B uses repetition (‘We are … asking’) to contrast a huge problem with a small request, which makes the request hard to refuse.

questions.prompt: A student begins a speech about a skate park with a famous quotation from a world leader that has little to do with the topic. What did the June 2023 Paper 2 examiner report say about this kind of opening?
options: Shoe-horned quotations added little; ideas linked to the topic and audience work better.
Famous quotations guarantee Level 4.
Every speech must start with a quotation.
The report praised this approach.
questions.explanation: The 2023 report noted quotations from famous figures being forced into answers, along with pre-prepared templates.
questions.misconception: Forcing a famous quotation into an answer to sound impressive.

questions.prompt: Why does Daniel say “I understand why” about young people being moved on?
options: It shows fairness to the councillors’ point of view, which makes his request harder to dismiss.
He agrees young people should be banned from the town.
He is changing the subject.
He wants to end the speech.
questions.explanation: By recognising the other side, Daniel presents himself as reasonable, so his argument gains credibility.

questions.prompt: A student turns the speech into an essay but keeps ‘Good evening, councillors’ and ‘Thank you for listening’. What is wrong?
options: These are spoken conventions; an essay needs a written opening and conclusion.
Essays must begin with ‘Dear Sir’.
Nothing is wrong.
Essays cannot mention councils.
questions.explanation: Each form has its own conventions. Carrying speech features into an essay shows the form has not been fully adapted.

questions.prompt: Rewrite lines 5 to 8 of the speech as a paragraph of a formal essay.
questions.model: Model answer (Level 4): In many towns, young people have few places to spend time after school. Benches outside shops and car parks near stations become meeting points by default, and those who gather there are often moved on. Such responses may be understandable, but they do not address the underlying problem: the lack of a space designed for young people to use.
checklist: Removes direct address and rhetorical questions
Uses a more impersonal, formal register
Keeps the original argument
Uses accurate punctuation and complex sentences
questions.explanation: Changing form changes the voice: the essay states and reasons where the speech appeals and asks.

questions.prompt: Write a speech for a school assembly arguing for or against this statement: ‘Every student should do 1 hour of volunteering each week.’ In the exam this task is worth 40 marks; here, write about 180 words.
questions.model:
Model answer (Level 4): Good morning, everyone. Last spring I spent my Saturday mornings at the food bank on Victoria Road. I went because my mum made me. I kept going because, for the first time in ages, I felt useful.

That is why I believe every student here should give 1 hour a week to volunteering. Just 1 hour. That is less time than most of us spend scrolling before breakfast.

Some of you are thinking: I already have homework and a job. You are right, and for some people even an hour is hard. So let the school help. Let volunteering count during the day, through a lunchtime club, or a reading scheme with the primary school down the road.

Volunteering is not about being a saint. It is about finding out what you are good at, and meeting people you would never otherwise meet. I found both on Victoria Road.

So give it 1 hour. You might find you want to give 2. Thank you.
checklist: Uses speech features such as direct address and a closing appeal
Presents a clear, convincing viewpoint
Answers a likely objection from the audience
Uses a register suited to a school assembly
Varies sentences and punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: Level 4 speeches sound like a real person talking to a real audience, with a clear argument and controlled structure.

units.title: Sentence demarcation and commas
units.summary: Mark every sentence with a capital letter and a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. Never join 2 sentences with a comma alone; use commas for lists, fronted adverbials and extra information.

questions.prompt: Which is correctly punctuated?
options: ‘The rain stopped. We went outside.’
‘The rain stopped, we went outside.’
‘the rain stopped we went outside’
‘The rain stopped we went outside.’
questions.explanation: Each main clause here is a complete sentence, so each needs its own capital letter and full stop. The second option is a comma splice.

questions.prompt: Why is there a comma after “Last Saturday” in line 1?
options: It follows a fronted adverbial at the start of the sentence.
It separates items in a list.
It marks direct speech.
It replaces a full stop.
questions.explanation: A phrase telling us when, where or how, placed at the front of a sentence, is usually followed by a comma.

questions.prompt: Choose all the sentences that contain a comma splice.
options: ‘The litter pick was busy, we filled 63 bags.’
‘Although it rained, we kept going.’
‘Maisie was 7, she was the youngest.’
‘We found a trolley, a wheel, a gnome and a boot.’
‘When the rain came, we went inside.’
questions.explanation: A comma splice joins 2 main clauses with only a comma. The second and fifth sentences start with a subordinate clause, and the fourth is a list.

questions.prompt: In line 4, the commas around “who has organised the event for 6 years” show:
options: extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence
a list of 3 people
the start of a new sentence
words someone spoke
questions.explanation: Commas in pairs mark an embedded clause. Remove it and ‘Mr Hussain handed out gloves …’ still works.

questions.prompt:
Which version is more secure?
Version A: ‘The forecast promised rain, the sky stayed clear, we worked until lunch.’
Version B: ‘Although the forecast promised rain, the sky stayed clear, so we worked until lunch.’
options: Version A, because it is shorter.
Version B, because the clauses are joined correctly with ‘although’ and ‘so’.
Version A, because commas can join any clauses.
Both are equally secure.
questions.explanation: Version A strings main clauses together with commas. Version B uses conjunctions so the commas are correct.

questions.prompt: The November 2024 Paper 2 examiner report noted a particular kind of technical error in Question 5. Which?
options: sentence demarcation errors, such as comma splices
too many paragraphs
using British spelling
writing in the first person
questions.explanation: The November 2024 report listed demarcation and agreement errors in Question 5. Secure demarcation is one of the first things AO6 rewards.
questions.misconception: Using commas where full stops are needed.

questions.prompt: Add the missing punctuation mark so that the sentence is correct: ‘By midday we had filled 63 bags___ most of the rubbish was plastic.’
questions.explanation: The next word starts with a small letter, so a full stop would be wrong. A semicolon joins 2 closely related main clauses; ‘, and’ would also work.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this sentence? ‘Mr Hussain, handed out gloves and bags.’
options: There should be no comma between the subject and its verb.
A comma is missing after ‘gloves’.
‘Hussain’ should not have a capital letter.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: A single comma between a subject and its verb splits the sentence for no reason. Commas come in pairs around extra information, as in line 4.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite this run-on passage with correct sentence demarcation:
‘the café was warm the owner gave us tea we stayed until the rain stopped then we went home’
questions.model: Model answer: The café was warm. The owner gave us tea, and we stayed until the rain stopped. Then we went home.
checklist: Starts each sentence with a capital letter
Ends each sentence with a full stop
Avoids comma splices
Uses a conjunction or full stop to join or separate clauses correctly
questions.explanation: There are several correct versions. What matters is that each main clause is either its own sentence or properly joined.

questions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (about 60 words) about a community event. Include at least 1 fronted adverbial, 1 embedded clause between commas and 1 list, all punctuated correctly.
questions.model: Model answer: On the first Sunday in May, the street held its annual plant sale. Mrs Okoro, who grows tomatoes in every window of her flat, sold out by 10am. Tables were covered with herbs, seedlings, cuttings and jam jars of sweet peas. When the stalls packed up, everyone agreed it had been the best year yet.
checklist: Includes a fronted adverbial followed by a comma
Includes an embedded clause marked by a pair of commas
Includes a correctly punctuated list
Contains no comma splices
Uses capital letters and full stops correctly
questions.explanation: Commas have specific jobs. Using each one deliberately shows the control that AO6 rewards.

units.title: Apostrophes
units.summary: An apostrophe does 2 jobs only: it shows missing letters (it’s = it is) and possession (the bakery’s ovens). Plurals and possessive ‘its’ never need one.

questions.prompt: Which are the 2 jobs an apostrophe does?
options: omission and possession
plurals and possession
omission and plurals
questions and exclamations
questions.explanation: Apostrophes show missing letters or ownership. They are never used just to make a plural.

questions.prompt: In line 2, what does “It’s easy” mean?
options: It is easy
It has easy
Its easy
It was easy
questions.explanation: The apostrophe marks the missing letter i in ‘it is’.

questions.prompt: Why is there no apostrophe in “its bread” (line 2)?
options: ‘its’ meaning ‘belonging to it’ never takes an apostrophe
The writer forgot it
Bread is uncountable
‘its’ is a plural
questions.explanation: ‘its’ is a possessive like ‘his’ and ‘her’, which also have no apostrophe. ‘it’s’ always means ‘it is’ or ‘it has’.

questions.prompt: Match each phrase from the text to its meaning.
pairs: recipes belonging to more than 1 parent
the uniforms of the staff as a group
questions.explanation: For a plural ending in s, the apostrophe goes after the s (parents’). For a plural not ending in s, add ’s (children’s).

questions.prompt:
Which sentence is more accurate?
Sentence A: ‘The baker’s bake bread every day and it’s smell fills the street.’
Sentence B: ‘The bakers bake bread every day and its smell fills the street.’
options: Sentence A, because it uses more apostrophes.
Sentence B, because ‘bakers’ is a simple plural and ‘its’ is possessive.
Sentence A, because ‘it’s’ is always correct.
Both are equally accurate.
questions.explanation: Sentence A adds an apostrophe to a plural and uses ‘it’s’ where ‘its’ is needed.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The 2 village’s were quiet.’ What is wrong?
options: A plural does not need an apostrophe: ‘villages’.
It should be ‘villages’’.
‘quiet’ should be ‘quite’.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: The June 2024 Paper 1 examiner report listed apostrophe errors among the technical weaknesses in Question 5. Adding an apostrophe to a plain plural is one of the most common.
questions.misconception: Using an apostrophe to make a plural.

questions.prompt: Choose all the sentences that use apostrophes correctly.
options: ‘The dog wagged its tail.’
‘Its raining again.’
‘The girls’ changing room is on the left.’
‘We bought 3 loaf’s.’
‘Who’d make the buns?’
questions.explanation: ‘Its raining’ needs it’s (it is). ‘loaf’s’ should be the plural ‘loaves’ with no apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Joan says, “Who’d make the buns?” (lines 15 to 16). What does ‘Who’d’ stand for here?
options: Who would
Who had
Who did
Whose
questions.explanation: ‘’d’ can stand for ‘had’ or ‘would’. Here she is imagining the future, so it means ‘would’.

questions.prompt:
Correct the apostrophes in this sentence:
‘Its the bakerys 50th birthday, and its owner’s are planning a party for the towns children.’
questions.model: Model answer: It’s the bakery’s 50th birthday, and its owners are planning a party for the town’s children.
checklist: Adds the apostrophe for omission in ‘It’s’
Adds the possessive apostrophe in ‘bakery’s’ and ‘town’s’
Removes the wrong apostrophe from the plural ‘owners’
Leaves possessive ‘its’ without an apostrophe
questions.explanation: Check each word: is a letter missing, does something belong to someone, or is it just a plural?

questions.prompt: Write 4 sentences about a local shop: 1 using an apostrophe for omission, 1 for singular possession, 1 for plural possession and 1 using ‘its’ correctly.
questions.model: Model answer: We’re lucky to have a hardware shop on our street. The owner’s dog sleeps in the doorway all day. On Saturdays the shop sells the local farmers’ eggs. Its window is full of buckets and seed packets.
checklist: Uses an apostrophe for omission correctly
Uses a singular possessive apostrophe correctly
Uses a plural possessive apostrophe correctly
Uses possessive ‘its’ without an apostrophe
questions.explanation: Writing each type on purpose is the best way to make the rules automatic.

units.title: Semicolons, colons and brackets
units.summary: A semicolon joins 2 closely related main clauses. A colon introduces an explanation, example or list. Brackets hold extra information. Use them accurately or not at all.

questions.prompt: What does the semicolon in line 1 do?
options: It joins 2 closely related main clauses.
It introduces a list.
It marks speech.
It shows possession.
questions.explanation: Both halves could stand alone as sentences: ‘The maritime museum is small.’ and ‘It takes about 2 hours …’. The semicolon shows they are closely linked.

questions.prompt: What does the colon in line 3 introduce?
options: an explanation of which exhibit stopped the group
a list of museums
a question
the end of the paragraph
questions.explanation: After the colon comes the thing promised in the first half: the sailor’s letter.

questions.prompt: Why are brackets used in lines 5 to 6?
options: to add extra information that the sentence could do without
to show speech
to mark a quotation
to join 2 sentences
questions.explanation: Remove the bracketed words and the sentence still works. The brackets hold a helpful aside.

questions.prompt: Choose all the sentences that use a semicolon correctly.
options: ‘The museum is small; it is worth a visit.’
‘The museum is small; and worth a visit.’
‘The guided walk is better; the volunteers know more.’
‘Because it rained; we stayed inside.’
questions.explanation: A semicolon needs a complete main clause on each side. ‘and worth a visit’ and ‘Because it rained’ cannot stand alone.

questions.prompt:
Which sentence is more accurate?
Sentence A: ‘The exhibit was: a letter from a sailor.’
Sentence B: ‘One exhibit held everyone’s attention: a sailor’s letter home.’
options: Sentence A, because it uses a colon.
Sentence B, because the colon follows a complete clause and introduces what it promised.
Sentence A, because it is shorter.
Both are equally accurate.
questions.explanation: A colon usually follows a complete main clause. In Sentence A the words before the colon do not make a sentence.

questions.prompt: What did the June 2019 Paper 2 examiner report say about semicolons and colons in Question 5?
options: They were more often used wrongly than correctly.
Each one used earned an extra mark.
They were banned.
Students did not use them at all.
questions.explanation: The June 2019 Paper 2 report found semicolons and colons more often wrong than right, and the Paper 1 report that year noted them used indiscriminately.
questions.misconception: Using semicolons and colons to impress, without being sure of the rules.

questions.prompt: Add the correct punctuation mark: ‘The museum offers 2 kinds of tour___ a guided walk and an audio guide.’
questions.explanation: The first half is complete and the second half explains it, so a colon is right. This is the same structure as line 7.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this sentence? ‘The diver’s helmet (it is heavier than it looks is on the top floor.’
options: The closing bracket is missing.
There should be no apostrophe in ‘diver’s’.
‘heavier’ is spelt wrongly.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: Brackets always come in pairs. Without the closing bracket, the reader cannot tell where the aside ends.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite these sentences using a semicolon and a colon correctly:
‘The museum was busy. We still enjoyed it. There was one exhibit I will never forget. It was a sailor’s letter.’
questions.model: Model answer: The museum was busy; we still enjoyed it. There was one exhibit I will never forget: a sailor’s letter.
checklist: Uses a semicolon between 2 related main clauses
Uses a colon after a complete clause to introduce what follows
Keeps the meaning of the original
Uses capital letters and full stops correctly
questions.explanation: Each mark should do a job that a full stop could not do as well.

questions.prompt: Write a short review (about 60 words) of a place you have visited. Use at least 1 colon and 1 semicolon accurately; brackets are optional.
questions.model: Model answer: The castle is not large; you can walk the walls in 20 minutes. Its best feature is easy to miss: a narrow staircase behind the chapel that leads to the old kitchens. Take a torch (the lighting is dim) and look for the bread oven. The café is fine, but the view from the walls is better.
checklist: Uses a semicolon correctly between main clauses
Uses a colon correctly to introduce an explanation or example
If brackets are used, they come in a pair around removable information
Writes in the style of a review
Contains no other punctuation errors
questions.explanation: Accurate advanced punctuation, used where it helps, is part of what lifts AO6 towards the top level.

units.title: Punctuating speech
units.summary: Put spoken words inside speech marks, start them with a capital letter and keep the punctuation that ends them inside the marks. Start a new line for each new speaker, and use dialogue sparingly.

questions.prompt: In line 3, where is the comma placed?
options: inside the speech marks, before the closing mark
outside the speech marks, after the closing mark
before the opening speech mark
there is no comma
questions.explanation: The punctuation that ends the spoken words goes inside the speech marks: "You could have answered your phone," she said.

questions.prompt: Decide whether each rule for punctuating speech is true or false.

statements.s: Each new speaker starts on a new line.
Spoken words begin with a capital letter.
The full stop at the end of speech goes outside the speech marks.
After a comma inside speech marks, ‘she said’ starts with a capital letter.

questions.explanation: The end punctuation stays inside the marks, and ‘she said’ continues the same sentence, so it takes a small letter.

questions.prompt: Which line is punctuated correctly?
options: ‘"Come on," she said.’
‘"Come on." She said.’
‘"Come on" she said.’
‘"Come on," She said.’
questions.explanation: A comma inside the marks, then a small letter for ‘she said’, then a full stop.

questions.prompt: In line 6, why is there a comma after “Then he said”?
options: A comma introduces speech that follows a reporting clause.
It separates items in a list.
It replaces a full stop.
It shows possession.
questions.explanation: When the reporting clause comes first, a comma separates it from the opening speech mark.

questions.prompt:
Which version is set out correctly?
Version A: ‘"You could have answered your phone," she said. Sami did not look up. "It died." "Mum has rung me 6 times."’ all on one line.
Version B: each speaker’s words start on a new line, as in lines 3 to 5 of the text.
options: Version A, because it saves space.
Version B, because a new line for each speaker makes it clear who is talking.
Version A, because speech should be grouped together.
Both are equally correct.
questions.explanation: Starting a new line when the speaker changes is a basic convention of dialogue, and it stops the reader losing track.

questions.prompt: What have examiners said about direct speech in Paper 1 Question 5 stories?
options: Long stretches of dialogue weakened many stories; use speech sparingly and punctuate it accurately.
Stories should be written entirely in dialogue.
Speech punctuation is not marked.
Dialogue always raises the AO5 mark.
questions.explanation: The June 2022 Paper 1 examiner report noted long stretches of direct speech, and the June 2024 report noted both too much speech and insecure speech punctuation.
questions.misconception: Filling a story with dialogue instead of narrative.

questions.prompt: Put these parts in order to make a correctly punctuated sentence.
items: "I didn’t get in,"
he said,
staring at the track.
"Not this year."
questions.explanation: The speech, then the reporting clause with a comma, then the action, then a new sentence of speech with its own capital letter.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this line? ‘"Mum has rung me 6 times" she said "what happened?"’
options: Punctuation is missing around ‘she said’, and the new sentence of speech needs a capital letter.
‘Mum’ should not have a capital letter.
The numeral should be a word.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: It should read: "Mum has rung me 6 times," she said. "What happened?" Compare line 5 of the text.

questions.prompt:
Punctuate this dialogue correctly, setting it out on new lines:
where are you going asked Nadia home said Sami i’m tired
questions.model:
Model answer:
"Where are you going?" asked Nadia.
"Home," said Sami. "I’m tired."
checklist: Puts each spoken part inside speech marks
Uses a question mark inside the marks for the question
Starts a new line for the new speaker
Uses a capital letter at the start of each new sentence of speech, including ‘I’m’
questions.explanation: Each speaker gets a new line, and each sentence of speech starts with a capital letter.

questions.prompt: Continue the scene with 4 to 6 lines of dialogue between Nadia and Sami. Punctuate it correctly and include at least 1 sentence of speech split by a reporting clause.
questions.model:
Model answer:
"Do you want to tell Mum," Nadia asked, "or shall I?"
Sami pulled his hood up. "You do it."
"She won’t be angry, you know."
"I know." He kicked at a crisp packet. "That’s almost worse."
The train finally appeared round the bend, and neither of them said anything else.
checklist: Starts a new line for each speaker
Keeps end punctuation inside the speech marks
Punctuates a split sentence of speech correctly, with a small letter after the reporting clause
Uses capital letters for new sentences of speech
Balances dialogue with some narrative
questions.explanation: Short, controlled dialogue with accurate punctuation is far more effective than long exchanges.

units.title: Agreement and Standard English
units.summary: Verbs must agree with their subjects (we were, the queue is). Use Standard English in formal writing: ‘should have’, not ‘should of’; ‘those students’, not ‘them students’.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is in Standard English?
options: ‘We were pleased.’
‘We was pleased.’
‘We be pleased.’
‘Us was pleased.’
questions.explanation: With ‘we’, the past tense of ‘be’ is ‘were’, as in line 3 of the report.

questions.prompt: Why do lines 12 to 13 say “fewer students” rather than ‘less students’?
options: ‘fewer’ is used with things you can count
‘less’ is never correct
‘fewer’ is more informal
Students are uncountable
questions.explanation: You can count students, so formal writing uses ‘fewer’. ‘Less’ goes with amounts you cannot count, such as ‘less noise’.

questions.prompt: Which verb agrees with its subject? ‘Each year group ___ a set time to queue.’
options: has
have
are having
were having
questions.explanation: ‘Each’ refers to 1 year group at a time, so the verb is singular: ‘has’.

questions.prompt: Choose all the sentences written in Standard English.
options: ‘We should have asked earlier.’
‘We should of asked earlier.’
‘The students were happy.’
‘The students was happy.’
‘Neither change is expensive.’
questions.explanation: ‘should of’ is a mishearing of ‘should’ve’, and a plural subject needs ‘were’.

questions.prompt:
Which sentence suits the student council report better?
Sentence A: ‘Loads of kids reckon the queue is well long.’
Sentence B: ‘Many students said the queue was too long.’
options: Sentence A, because it sounds natural.
Sentence B, because its formal register suits a report to the head teacher.
Sentence A, because it is more vivid.
Both are equally suitable.
questions.explanation: A report to a head teacher needs Standard English and a formal register.

questions.prompt: A student writes: ‘The queue for the hot meals are too long.’ What is wrong?
options: The verb should agree with ‘queue’, which is singular: ‘is’.
‘meals’ should be ‘meal’.
‘too’ should be ‘to’.
Nothing is wrong.
questions.explanation: The verb has been made to agree with the nearest noun, ‘meals’, instead of the subject, ‘queue’. The June 2019 Paper 2 examiner report noted agreement errors in Question 5.
questions.misconception: Making the verb agree with the nearest noun instead of the subject.

questions.prompt: Match each non-standard form to its Standard English version.
questions.explanation: These are among the most common non-standard forms in exam writing. Learn the standard versions so they become automatic.

questions.prompt: A student changes the report’s last paragraph to: ‘Neither of these changes are expensive.’ Which version is preferred in formal writing?
options: ‘Neither of these changes is expensive.’
‘Neither of these changes be expensive.’
‘Neither of these change are expensive.’
The student’s version is preferred.
questions.explanation: In formal writing, ‘neither’ is treated as singular, so it takes ‘is’. The report itself avoids the problem with “would be”.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite this in Standard English for a formal report:
‘Me and my mates was asked about the canteen. We done the survey and loads of us said the food were alright but the queue is massive.’
questions.model: Model answer: My friends and I were asked about the canteen. We completed the survey, and many of us said the food was acceptable but the queue was far too long.
checklist: Corrects ‘Me and my mates was’ to a standard subject and verb
Replaces ‘done’ with a standard past tense
Makes ‘food’ agree with ‘was’
Replaces informal words such as ‘loads’ and ‘massive’
Keeps tenses consistent
questions.explanation: Standard English is about grammar; formal register is about word choice. A report needs both.

questions.prompt: Write a short formal paragraph (about 60 words) for a report to your head teacher about improving the school library. Use Standard English throughout.
questions.model: Model answer: The library is popular at lunchtime, but there are fewer seats than students who wish to use them. We recommend adding 2 more tables near the windows. In addition, many students would like the library to stay open until 4.30pm, so that those who wait for later buses have somewhere quiet to work. These changes would cost little.
checklist: Uses Standard English grammar throughout
Makes every verb agree with its subject
Uses a formal register suited to a report
Organises points clearly
Spells and punctuates accurately
questions.explanation: Formal reports reward standard grammar and a calm, polite tone.

units.title: Spelling: homophones and exam words
units.summary: Homophones sound the same but are spelt differently: their, there, they’re; affect, effect; practice, practise. Learn the difference so you can check them in the last few minutes.

questions.prompt: Which word completes this sentence correctly? ‘The weather can ___ the whole day.’
options: affect
effect
affects
effects
questions.explanation: ‘Affect’ is usually the verb (to have an influence on); ‘effect’ is usually the noun (the result). Line 3 uses ‘affect’.

questions.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the conditions outside, such as rain or wind
in that place, or as in ‘there is’
questions.explanation: Each pair sounds alike, so the meaning is the only guide to the spelling.

questions.prompt: In line 7, why is it “practise” with an s?
options: In British English, ‘practise’ is the verb and ‘practice’ is the noun.
It is the American spelling.
‘practise’ is always correct.
It is a mistake.
questions.explanation: The students practise (verb) their French. A football practice (noun) takes a c.

questions.prompt: Choose ‘lose’ or ‘loose’ to complete the sentence: ‘Don’t ___ your slip.’
questions.explanation: ‘lose’ (one o) means to misplace; ‘loose’ (double o) means not tight, as in “a loose sail” in line 6.

questions.prompt:
Which sentence is spelt correctly?
Sentence A: ‘Their going to the coast weather or not it rains.’
Sentence B: ‘They’re going to the coast whether or not it rains.’
options: Sentence A
Sentence B
Both
Neither
questions.explanation: ‘They’re’ means ‘they are’, and ‘whether’ introduces alternatives. Sentence A confuses both pairs.

questions.prompt: The June 2024 Paper 1 examiner report noted a student writing about hot ‘desserts’. Which spelling is correct for dry, sandy regions?
options: deserts
desserts
dessarts
desirts
questions.explanation: ‘Desserts’ are puddings; ‘deserts’ are dry regions. A spelling slip like this can change the meaning, which is why proofreading matters.
questions.misconception: Confusing words that differ by a single letter, such as deserts and desserts.

questions.prompt: Choose all the sentences that are spelt correctly.
options: ‘The effect of the wind was dramatic.’
‘You’re coat is on the bus.’
‘We were wondering where to go.’
‘The sail was lose.’
‘It’s definitely going to rain.’
questions.explanation: ‘You’re’ means ‘you are’, so it should be ‘Your coat’. ‘lose’ should be ‘loose’ (not tight).

questions.prompt: Choose the 2 words that are spelt wrongly in this sentence: ‘The teachers new that the strong wind would effect the sailing.’
options: teachers
new
strong
effect
sailing
questions.explanation: It should be ‘knew’ (past tense of know) and ‘affect’ (the verb).

questions.prompt:
Correct the 5 errors in this sentence:
‘Wen we arrived, there was know sign of the boat. Its sail was lose and there instructor said we would of been safer in the museum.’
questions.model: Model answer: When we arrived, there was no sign of the boat. Its sail was loose and their instructor said we would have been safer in the museum.
checklist: Corrects ‘Wen’ to ‘When’
Corrects ‘know’ to ‘no’
Corrects ‘lose’ to ‘loose’
Corrects ‘there’ to ‘their’
Corrects ‘would of’ to ‘would have’
questions.explanation: ‘Its sail’ was already correct: the sail belongs to the boat, so possessive ‘its’ needs no apostrophe.

questions.prompt: Write a short paragraph (about 60 words) about a school trip that uses each of these words correctly: affect, effect, their, there, practise.
questions.model: Model answer: On the drama trip, the actors showed us how lighting can affect the mood of a scene. The effect of a single blue spotlight was eerie. There was time afterwards to practise our own scenes on the real stage. The actors watched and gave their advice, and we left feeling far more confident.
checklist: Uses ‘affect’ as a verb
Uses ‘effect’ as a noun
Uses ‘their’ for possession and ‘there’ for place or ‘there was’
Uses ‘practise’ as a verb
Spells all other words correctly
questions.explanation: Using each word in context is the surest way to fix the right spelling in your memory.
